response.body:
Adds a reconcile pass to the session-decisions queue, following [#105](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/105).

## What it does

- **`/decisions reconcile`** prints the open items as a table (label, kind, how long each has waited and when it was last revised, link, text with the recommendation), followed by every line of the user's own messages that names one of those labels (`A116: done`, `D3: go with zfs`, `re D3, raidz2 after all`). The same brief goes to the model as the command's note (`context`), and a short reconcile request is submitted to start the turn.
- **`decision_list` tool** returns the same brief, so the assistant can reconcile when asked in plain words, and no longer has to rebuild the open set from reminders.
- **Skill: "Reconciling the queue"** has the assistant check each item for evidence (the user's words by label or subject, the state of a linked PR or issue checked now, or a later item that supersedes it), propose close / update / keep in one table with an evidence column, change nothing until the user answers, then apply every approved change in one message. A close needs the user's words or a linked forge state; keep is the answer whenever the evidence is ambiguous.

## Choices where the issue left room

- **Command shape:** a mode of the existing command (`/decisions reconcile`), next to `wrap`, rather than a new command.
- **Evidence gathering:** the plugin collects only the deterministic part, which is the user's lines that name a label. It skips the plugin's own reminder, its reconcile and wrap prompts, the compaction summary, and lines that only repeat the queue, and keeps the newest three per label. Matching by subject, checking forge state and spotting a superseding item are left to the assistant, which is the one that can judge them.
- **"One batch":** task-list items can only change through TaskUpdate, and the plugin doesn't write task files. So "one batch" here means a single message with every TaskUpdate (or `decision_close` / `decision_update` for ledger items) as parallel calls after one approval. I didn't add a batch tool.
- **Brief shown once:** the brief goes out as the command's output and its model note. Putting it in the submitted prompt would have printed the table twice.

## Fix along the way

The host refuses `$.prompt.submit` from inside a `command.run` hook (`it would wait on the turn this hook is holding`), and the call's rejection was caught and dropped. So `/decisions wrap` never actually sent its prompt. Both `wrap` and `reconcile` now submit from a `$.clock.after(0, …)` timer once the command has answered, and a refusal shows as a toast. There's a test for each.

## Checks

- `claude plugin test plugins/session-decisions`: 128 pass (new `tests/reconcile.test.ts`, plus register tests for the command, the wrap fix and `decision_list`).
- `claude plugin validate --strict plugins/session-decisions` and the marketplace: pass.
- I drove a real Claude Code session with term-recorder (Haiku, plugin from this branch) at 100x30 and 60x30: create D1 and A1, answer `A1: done`, run `/decisions reconcile`. The brief printed, the deferred prompt started the turn, and the assistant answered with one table proposing close A1 (quoting `A1: done`) and keep D1 (no evidence).

Closes #105
response.title: feat(session-decisions): reconcile open items against the session

response.body:
Long sessions accumulate stale queue items. In a lokkju/infra session on 2026-10-20 and 21, items stayed open after the work behind them was done or overtaken: D141 was answered in conversation but sat open until a later turn noticed; D157's question changed four times as the operator added disks, and was settled in conversation without a ruling recorded; A-items the operator completed ("A116: done") had to be closed one call at a time. The operator had to ask for a manual cleanup pass.

Ask: a reconcile step, as a skill or command (say `/decisions-reconcile`, or a mode of the existing skill), that:

1. Lists every open item with its label, age and text.
2. For each, checks the session for evidence it's settled: the operator's own words answering it (by label or by subject), a merged PR or closed issue the item links to, or a later item that supersedes it.
3. Proposes, in one table, close (with the ruling quoted from the operator's message), update (new text when the question or recommendation drifted), or keep, and applies the operator's yes in one batch rather than one tool call per item.
4. Never closes an item on the agent's own say-so: a close needs the operator's words or a linked forge state, and a keep is the default when evidence is ambiguous.

It would also help to have a list action on the tool side (open items with label, kind, age, link), since today the agent reconstructs the open set from the session's reminders.

Related: [#99](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/99) (the hand-off check), [#104](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/104) (chat rendering), [#14](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/14) (revising items when context changes).
response.title: session-decisions: a reconcile step that checks open items against the session and closes or revises them in one pass

The mod in [#107](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/107) wasn't missing because of anything in this plugin. The job ran in a folder Claude Code hadn't been told to trust, and Claude Code ran it without any hooks at all.

What the transcript and logs show for job `651f1ed2`:

- `~/projects/agentsview` was cloned at 02:40:21 UTC on 2026-10-22, and the job claimed its spare process at 02:40:48 (`daemon.log`, launched from the shell). Nobody had accepted the folder's trust prompt yet.
- For the whole 2.1.302 run, no SessionStart hook ran: not this plugin's and not session-history's plain command hook either. Plugin MCP servers and skills loaded, which is why the skill was there and the mod wasn't.
- `872c2311`, another 2.1.302 background job started an hour later in the trusted `~/projects/infra`, ran SessionStart:startup hooks and had `decision_add` from its first turn. The same installed plugin (2026.10.18.1, cache intact, every import present) loaded fine there.
- After the folder was trusted and the job resumed on 2.1.306, this plugin's SessionStart context and the `decision_add` tools showed up in the same session.
- Reproduced on 2.1.306: `claude --bg` in a fresh, untrusted git folder now refuses to start, with "Workspace not trusted. Run `claude` in ... once and accept the trust prompt, then retry." The same prompt from a trusted folder got the tools. So 2.1.306 already closes the hole that 2.1.302 let the job through.

Nothing in `plugin.json` or `hooks.json` needs to change, and `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TODO_TOOLS` and deferred tools play no part.

What this changes:

- The skill now covers the case where tool search finds neither TaskCreate nor `decision_add`: tell the user once, number items from D1 and A1, end each reply that leaves items open with an `Open items` list, restate it at hand-off, and create the items in the queue if the tools turn up later.
- The README's Requirements section says function hooks need workspace trust, what 2.1.302 and 2.1.306 do with an untrusted background job, and that resuming after trusting the folder loads the plugin.

`claude plugin validate --strict` and `claude plugin test` pass (121 tests).

response.body:
On a card, the last line of text before `[more]` is sometimes the same color as `[more]`, so the button doesn't read as a separate control.

**Cause** (`hooks/register.tsx` on main, the card renderer): `[more]` is a `Button` with `plain dimColor`. It follows whichever line of text comes last, and when an item has a recommendation qualifier, that's the qualifier line. The qualifier is drawn `dimColor` on purpose, as secondary text. So in that case the text and `[more]` share one dim style, and `[more]` looks like the end of the sentence. When `[more]` follows the question instead, the text is drawn at normal weight and the two are easy to tell apart.

**Fix:** give `[more]` a style that stays distinct from both normal and dim text, in every case. Use the accent color the card already uses for the next item's border (`ACCENT`), or underline, and keep its hover bold. Check it on screen with term-recorder at 100x30 and 60x30 for three kinds of item: one with a qualifier, one without, and one where `[more]` goes on its own row. Look in both the pane and the details view.

response.body:
Three queue misses in one long session (eltoro-drop, 2026-10-21, session-decisions 2026.10.20.1), all the same shape, and the shape is not the one the skill is written for.

## The measurement

54 queue items by the end: 31 `DECIDE`, 23 `ACTION`.

**Every miss was an `ACTION`. Not one `DECIDE` was missed.**

1. **The client secret.** Putting a Keycloak client secret in Vault was the only thing blocking the restart of a ~20h index build against a hard regulatory deadline. I identified it, researched where it should go, recommended a path with its blast-radius caveat — in prose — and never created an item. It stayed unqueued across a compaction and roughly a dozen turns, during which I did hours of unrelated implementation work.
2. **The push approval.** Nine commits needed a Bitwarden SSH prompt answered. Never queued.
3. **The fix for (1) and (2).** Asked to diagnose the failure, I wrote the analysis and ended with "*(A24 is in the queue for that so it doesn't become the next thing I only mention.)*" **A24 did not exist.** I had not called `TaskCreate`. The user caught it.

(3) is the useful one. It happened one paragraph after I correctly described the failure mode, inside the message whose entire subject was that failure mode. Whatever is going on is not inattention and will not be fixed by a clearer rule.

## Cause

**The incentive is asymmetric, and the skill's framing follows the incentive rather than correcting it.**

A `DECIDE` blocks *the agent*. I cannot write the code until the user rules, so queueing it is how I get unblocked — the tool call is on the critical path of my own work and it never gets skipped.

An `ACTION` blocks *only the user*. I can route around it indefinitely, and nothing in my own loop goes red. That is literally what happened: I shipped two decisions' worth of implementation while the thing stopping the build sat in a paragraph.

The skill reinforces this. Its first heading is **"Before you ask"**, the worked guidance is about options and recommendations, and the trigger sentence is *"Every question you need answered, and every step only they can do"* — a question first, the action clause trailing. `ACTION` reads as the minor case. It is the one that fails.

Four things keep the miss invisible once it happens:

- **The prose shadow-queue.** I restate pending work in "what's next" closers, hand-off summaries, and — critically — in compaction summaries, which carried "Pending Tasks: client secret → Vault → env — the only thing blocking the build restart" as plain text. Restating it diligently makes it *feel* tracked. The better the narrative summary, the weaker the signal that the real queue is short an item. The compaction summary is a *competing* durable store, and it is the one I write without being asked.
- **Answer-shaped work.** The secret arrived as the answer to "what do you recommend?". I answered; the exchange felt closed. But an answer of "you need to put X in Y" *creates* an action rather than discharging one.
- **Routine.** The push approval had happened a dozen times that session. Repetition stops something reading as requiring the user, though every instance did.
- **Stating intent reads as having acted.** The A24 case. Writing "(A24 is in the queue)" is the same move as writing it into a summary: the sentence does the work the tool call should have, and nothing distinguishes the two from the inside.

## Why the existing guard did not catch it

**The skill already promises this check:**

> Anything you hand back to the user counts, including a merge or a step on their hosts that you could do yourself if asked: a reply that ends with "left for you" or "you'll need to" items that aren't queued gets flagged to the user, and you're reminded on the next turn.

It did not fire on any of the three, as far as I could tell — and replies said "the only thing blocking the build restart", "I cannot write to Vault for you", "say the word and I will start the push".

Meanwhile #99 reports the same check firing on a description and then on a *quotation of its own false positive*. Both of those are real false positives and worth fixing. But the two issues need reading together, because tuning only in #99's direction makes this one worse, and there is a well-known failure here: **a check that cries wolf is a check you stop reading, and then the true positives cost exactly what having no check costs.** Three misses with the check nominally live is the evidence.

So the question is not "make it quieter" or "make it louder". It is: what makes it *precise*, and what does it do when it fires?

## Potential fixes

Roughly in order of how much they buy.

**1. Make a fired hand-off check BLOCK, not inform.** Today it flags the user and reminds the agent next turn — by which point the reply has shipped, the user has read the prose, and the reminder competes with whatever they said next. A `Stop` hook that refuses the turn and quotes the matched phrase back puts the cost on the agent in the same turn, which is the only place it changes behaviour. One extra tool call to recover; the missed blocker in this session cost hours. This is the same argument the eltoro-drop `CLAUDE.md` makes about `cmd || echo` in a gate task: a leg that cannot fail is not a gate.

**2. Precision work, which #99 and this issue agree on from opposite sides.** Both of us want fewer false positives, and the fixes #99 proposes (ignore quoted text, ignore future-tense descriptions of another agent's output, require an action object) raise precision without lowering recall on any of my three misses. Worth adding as fixtures from this session, as true positives next to #99's true negatives:
   - "that is the only thing blocking the build restart" → must flag
   - "I cannot write to Vault for you" → must flag
   - "say the word and I will start the push" → must flag
   - "approve the prompt" → must flag
   - "(A24 is in the queue for that)" with no A24 in the list → must flag, as its own rule (see 4)

**3. Reorder the skill so `ACTION` is the first-class case.** Concretely: lead the trigger with the step-only-they-can-do clause, not the question clause; give `ACTION` its own worked example (today every example is a decision); and say explicitly that an action which does not block the agent is the one most likely to be dropped, with the reason. The skill is the thing I read every session, and right now it teaches the pattern that fails.

**4. Treat an item reference with no matching item as an error.** The skill already says *"In your message, refer to the item by its label ('D3'); TaskList shows it if TaskCreate's result doesn't."* Nothing enforces it. A check for `\b[DA]\d+\b` in the final message with no corresponding item would have caught A24 at zero cost and no ambiguity — it needs no NLP, it is an exact lookup, and it catches the specific move of asserting a queue state instead of creating it. I would start here: it is the cheapest rule in this list and it caught the subtlest of the three misses.

**5. Make the compaction summary carry the queue, or stop it carrying a copy.** The "Pending Tasks" section of a compaction summary is a second, unsynchronised task list that the agent writes unprompted and then trusts. Either the summary should be generated *from* the open items (so they cannot diverge), or the skill should say plainly that pending work in a summary is not tracked and must be queued — because the summary is exactly where an unqueued item goes to look safe.

**6. Nudge on content, not just staleness.** The existing reminder fires when the task tools go unused for a while. It fired repeatedly in this session and I read it as "no new decisions", which was true of decisions and false of actions. A nudge conditioned on *hand-off language in the previous turn with no `TaskCreate` since* would have fired at the right moment, with the right content, instead of as ambient noise.

## What I would not do

Add more prose to the skill telling the agent to be careful. The rule is already there, in plain language, and I read it every session and violated it three times in one day — the third time in the middle of writing down why. The eltoro-drop `CLAUDE.md` is a catalogue of guards that failed because their only enforcement was somebody remembering; this is the same species.

Related: #99 (the same check, over-firing), #105 (reconcile open items against the session).
response.title: session-decisions: ACTION items are the ones that go unqueued, and the hand-off check is being tuned toward missing them

response.body:
Two fixes to how session-decisions draws its items: queue items no longer print into the transcript twice ([#104](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/104)), and Back from the details view returns to where the list was ([#102](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/102)).

## #104: one line in the transcript

Of the three options in the issue, I went with a one-line mention: `● queued D3`, whose label opens the item in the queue pane. The issue asks for nothing, "or at most one short line (`queued D161`)", and the line is that. Drawing nothing at all would also hide the engine's own `decision_add(...)` row, so the transcript would have no mark of when the item was asked. On VS Code and mobile there's no footer count, and on the terminal's main screen the sidebar doesn't open by itself, so the line is the one way to get from the conversation to the item. It takes one row and never repeats the question.

- `ToolUse` for TaskCreate, `decision_add` and `decision_update`: one line, `queued D3`, or `revised D3` for `decision_update`. Once the item is settled it's the same dim `✓ D3 · <ruling>` line as before.
- `ToolResult` for those calls draws an empty box. The tool still returns the labelled subject, so the model reads exactly what it did before. Only the drawing changed.
- Under ctrl+o (`isExpanded`), both rows pass through to the engine, so the full call and result are still there.
- A folded `ToolGroup` draws the line under the group, where it used to draw the card.

The overflow: cards are no longer drawn in the transcript, which is where the issue saw one break its border. Where cards are still drawn (the pane), the last text row beside `[more]` now sits in a `flexShrink` box. If the width that row was measured at is more than the card actually has, the text wraps instead of pushing past the border. I couldn't reproduce the original overflow on 2.1.306 at 100 or 60 columns. My best guess is a transcript narrowed by the docked sidebar, so the measured width came out larger than the drawn one, but that's inferred, not verified.

Before (main, 100x30), the item twice:

```
╭──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮
│  ACTION  A1                                                                                   0m │
│ tell the codexpublicus session to (1) cargo clean or delete the target/ of every finished        │
│ worktree under ~/projects/codexpublicus (43 target dirs, 152G on /) and remove finished          │
│ worktrees, and (2) set up sccache so the next builds share one cache [more]                      │
│ [ Done ] [ Answer ]                                                                      no link │
╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯
  ⎿  A1 ACTION: tell the codexpublicus session to (1) `cargo clean` or delete the target/ of ev
     ery finished worktree under ~/projects/codexpublicus (43 target dirs, 152G on /) and remov
     e finished worktrees, and (2) set up sccache so the next builds share one cache [no link]
```

After, 15 `decision_add` calls in one message (the first is the long A117 text from the issue), at 100x30:

```
  [no link]' for N from 2 to 15. Reply only: ok
● queued A1
● queued A2
  ...
● queued A15

● ok
```

At 60x30 (resized):

```
  link]' for N from 2 to 15. Reply only: ok
● queued A1
● queued A2
  ...
● queued A15

● ok
                                            ● 15 decisions
```

TaskCreate, 100x30:

```
❯ Load TaskCreate with ToolSearch, then call TaskCreate once with subject 'DECIDE: share one
  sccache across worktrees? (recommend yes) [no link]' and description 'saves rebuilds'. Reply
  only: ok
● queued D1

● ok
```

The long card in the pane at 60x30 wraps inside its frame:

```
│ ╭──────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮ │
│ │  ACTION  A1                                       6m │ │
│ │ tell the codexpublicus session to (1) cargo clean or │ │
│ │ delete the target/ of every finished worktree under  │ │
│ │ ~/projects/codexpublicus (43 target dirs, 152G on    │ │
│ │ /) and remove finished worktrees, and (2) set up     │ │
```

## #102: Back keeps the list's place

Opening the details view scrolls the pane to its start. Back then asked to scroll to the item's card before the list had been drawn again, so the request found nothing and the list was left at the top. Now:

- The pane records the list's offset as the person scrolls it (a `ui.scroll` hook) and whenever the list draws.
- Back first focuses the item's label. `$.ui.focus` waits for the drawing that brings the label, so everything after it runs against the list, not the details view.
- It then scrolls to a one-cell marker that the list draws, absolutely positioned at the recorded offset, while Back runs. A plugin's `$.ui.scroll` takes an element, never a row number, and the plugin's own `ui.scroll` hook doesn't run on its own calls (I tried rewriting the offset there, and it never fired), so the marker is how it gets to an exact row.
- Last, it scrolls the item's card to `nearest`. That's a no-op when the card is already in view, and it shows the whole card when the recorded offset left part of it cut off.

Back from A9 in the 15-item list, 100x30, the pane in place below the prompt (before the details view, then after Back):

```
│ │ [ Done ] [ Answer ]                                                                  no link │ │
│ ╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯ │
│ ╭──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮ │
│ │  ACTION  A9                                                                               5m │ │
│ │ step 9 of the checklist [more]                                                               │ │
│ │ [ Done ] [ Answer ]                                                                  no link │ │
│ ╰──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╯ │
│ ╭──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────╮ │
```

The two screens are identical, row for row. Opening A14, whose card was cut off at the top of the window, and pressing Back lands two rows higher, with A14's card shown whole.

## Checks

- `claude plugin test plugins/session-decisions`: 110 pass. The transcript tests now check the one line, that the result row draws nothing, that ctrl+o passes both through, and that the line opens the item.
- `claude plugin validate --strict` on the plugin and the marketplace.
- `tsc` against the 2.1.306 declarations: clean.
- The test kit has no implementation of `$.ui.focus` or `$.ui.scroll` for a call made from a press ("no implementation for ui.focus"), so the Back offset is verified on screen only, not in a test.

Closes #104
Closes #102

response.body:
[#106](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/106) and [#99](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/99) pull the hand-off check in opposite directions, so this works them as one change: it raises precision on #99's false positives without dropping any of #106's misses, and catches the misses it used to let through. It stays a toast plus a next-turn reminder; nothing blocks the reply.

**Now flagged** (`hooks/handoff.ts`)

- User-only steps described in prose, the shape of every miss in #106: `the only thing blocking the build restart`, `I cannot write to Vault for you`, `I can't access …` / `I don't have access to …`, `say the word and I will start the push`, `approve the SSH key prompt`, `put the client secret in Vault …`, `the push needs your SSH key approval`, `the build is waiting on you`. The `you'll need to` / `for you to` / `please` verb lists gain the secret, prompt and account verbs (put, store, answer, unlock, accept, enter, pay and so on).
- A `D<n>`/`A<n>` the reply names that the session's queue doesn't hold (#106's A24 and D33). The Stop hook passes every label in the session, settled ones included, so a real label still covers its line and a dangling one is flagged whatever the wording. The toast reads `D33 named but not in the queue`, and the reminder says to create the item and to make the tool call before the sentence that names it. Look-alikes (`D3.js`) and labels in code or quotes don't count.

**No longer flagged**

- A trigger phrase inside straight or curly quotes or backticks, and a line that is mostly quotation. A command in a code span still counts (`you'll need to run \`…\``).
- A line about the check itself (`hand-off warning`, `false positive`, `not queued:`).
- A sentence about what another agent, a document or a tool will produce: `It'll lay out … the questions only you can answer`, `The report lists the steps you'll need to run`, `It prints the cleanup commands for you to run`. A future that waits on the user still counts (`it'll need your approval`, `that'll be your call`).
- `only you can answer/decide/know` with nothing after it. `only you can approve the merge` and `something only you can do` still count.
- `nothing you have to configure`, `what's waiting on you`.

**Skill text** (`SKILL.md`): it now opens with a section on actions only the user can take, ahead of the renamed "Before you ask a question". The section covers what counts, why actions go unqueued (they never block the assistant), the three ways they slip (arriving as a recommendation, being routine, already written into prose or a compaction summary), and an `ACTION` example. It also adds the sequencing rule from #106's comment: create the item before writing the sentence that names its label. The frontmatter description leads with steps that wait on the user.

**Fixtures** (`tests/handoff.test.ts`, `tests/register.test.tsx`)

- Must flag: eleven paraphrased #106 lines, the A24 and D33 lines with no matching item, and a label that isn't in the queue inside an otherwise covered hand-off line.
- Must not flag: #99's two lines (the description, and the false-positive note, quoted and unquoted), a third from the same session describing a feature that "prints the cleanup commands for you to run", quoted and backticked trigger phrases, descriptions of a report or agent, the same #106 steps once queued, hedged or done by the assistant, and known labels or look-alikes.
- All existing fixtures pass unchanged except one register test that named `A3` when only A1 and A2 existed. It now names `A2`, and a new register test covers the dangling-label toast and reminder.
- Before and after over every markdown file in the repo (paragraphs joined into reply-length lines): the only lines dropped were ones quoting the check's own phrases, and the only new hit was an imperative "store the client ID and key on the repo" in the forge-release docs, which is the kind of step this is meant to catch.

121 tests pass, and `claude plugin validate --strict plugins/session-decisions` passes.

Not done here: #106's fix 1 (block the turn instead of nudging) was left out on purpose, and fix 5 (generate the compaction summary from the queue) is only covered by the skill text.

Closes #106
Closes #99
response.title: fix(session-decisions): catch user-only steps and unqueued labels in the hand-off check

response.body:
The hand-off check from [#63](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/pull/63) flagged two lines in a row that weren't hand-offs. Both were on session-decisions 2026.10.20.1, on 2026-10-20.

1. A line describing what a research agent would produce: "It'll lay out two or three options with a recommendation and the questions only you can answer." The trigger was "only you can". The line describes the agent's planned output, not a step for the user.
2. The next reply's note about that false positive: "Hand-off warning false positive: … That line described the agent's planned output, not a step for you." It quoted the earlier phrase, so it tripped the same rule.

Both cost the user a reminder and the model a turn spent explaining that nothing needed queuing.

What would cut these out:
- **Don't count a trigger phrase inside quotes.** That covers straight and curly quotes, backticks, and a line that is mostly a quotation.
- **Don't count a trigger phrase in a future-tense description of someone else's output.** "It'll …", "the agent will …", "the report lists …" don't hand anything to the user. Only an imperative or obligation addressed to the user does: "you'll need to …", "run …", "merge …", "only you can …" said of a step.
- **Require an object that's an action.** "only you can" should count when it's followed by a verb phrase for something to do ("only you can approve the merge"), not by "answer" inside a description of questions.
- **Tests:** these two lines as fixtures that must not flag, next to the existing true positives.

Related: [#1](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/1).
response.title: session-decisions: the hand-off check flags descriptions and quotes, not just hand-offs

response.body:
A new plugin, `worktree-tidy`: a SessionStart hook that finds stale git worktrees and says so, and a `/worktree-tidy` skill that lists them with the commands to remove them. It only reads. Removal is the commands it prints, for you to run, since agents can't run `git worktree remove --force` and repos with submodules need it.

I made it its own plugin. forge-tracker's `/groom` is an on-demand tracker review, and this is a hook that has to run on every session start in any repo, GitHub-tracked or not; folding it into forge-tracker would make everyone who wants the nudge install the tracker workflow too.

**Stale** (listed with commands):
- merged / closed: the branch's newest PR merged (or closed), no PR from it is open, the branch is gone from the GitHub remote, the worktree's commit is in the PR, and `git status --porcelain --ignore-submodules=none` is empty.
- detached: clean, on a commit some branch or tag has, HEAD/index/reflog untouched for 7 days (`WORKTREE_TIDY_DETACHED_DAYS`).
- prunable: git already marks it prunable.

**Look at** (listed, no commands): merged but dirty, carrying commits the PR doesn't have, or with its branch still on the remote; detached and dirty or on an unreferenced commit; directories under `.claude/worktrees/` or `.wt/` that git doesn't list. Never listed: main checkouts, the session's own worktree, locked worktrees, branches with an open PR or none.

**Scope:** the session's repo (every worktree `git worktree list` shows), or every non-hidden repo one level down when the cwd isn't a repo; `WORKTREE_TIDY_ROOTS` overrides.

**GitHub:** one read-only `gh api graphql` query per repo for all its worktree branches (PRs plus `ref(refs/heads/…)`), over HTTPS, cached ten minutes under `$CLAUDE_PLUGIN_DATA`. If gh is missing or fails, those worktrees are "couldn't check PRs", never gone; the hook says so when it happens. `WORKTREE_TIDY_OFFLINE=1` skips GitHub.

**Budget:** 4 seconds for the hook (`WORKTREE_TIDY_BUDGET`), hook timeout 15; whatever the budget doesn't reach is reported as not reached, never classified.

**Commands:** one line per stale worktree, each guarded so it removes nothing that's become dirty since the report:
```
{ [ -z "$(git -C WT status --porcelain --ignore-submodules=none)" ] && git -C REPO worktree remove [--force] WT && git -C REPO branch -D BRANCH; } || echo 'worktree-tidy: left WT (not clean, or git refused)' >&2
git -C REPO worktree prune
```
`--force` only when the worktree has a `.gitmodules`.

**Read-only dry run** over `~/projects/skills` and `~/projects/codexpublicus` (9 repos, 54 linked worktrees): 28 stale (27 merged, 1 detached), all in skills; 22 to look at (15 merged with the branch still on the remote, 7 directories under `.wt/` git doesn't list). Cold run with GitHub queries 1.5 to 2.4 s; the hook with a warm cache 0.2 s on skills and 0.1 s on the codexpublicus folder.

Not done: the optional `Stop` hook and systemd sweep from the issue, and a removal command the agent runs itself (deliberately; the commands are for you).

Tests: 49, with temporary repos, worktrees, a submodule repo (checks git refuses removal without `--force` and the guarded line removes it), and a fake `gh`. The printed commands are executed in the tests to check they remove exactly what's listed and leave a worktree dirtied after the report.

Closes #103
response.title: feat(worktree-tidy): report stale git worktrees at session start

response.body:
Worktrees made for agent and PR work pile up after their PRs merge. On 2026-10-21 one sweep of the codexpublicus repos removed 67: 60 whose PRs had merged and 7 detached scratch checkouts. Nobody removed them after merging, and agents can't run `git worktree remove --force`, which repos with submodules require. Native `EnterWorktree` worktrees get cleaned up on exit; worktrees created with `git worktree add` (for example under a repo's `.wt/` when the session's cwd isn't a git repo) never do.

**Proposal: a hook that finds stale worktrees and reports them.**

- **When:** `SessionStart`, and optionally `Stop`, so a session that merged PRs sees what's now stale before it ends.
- **Scope:** the session's repo, or for a workspace directory every git repo one level down (configurable list of roots).
- **Stale means:** the worktree's branch is gone from the remote and its PR is merged or closed, or the worktree is detached with no changes and older than N days. Check remote state over HTTPS (`git ls-remote https://...`) or `gh`; if that returns nothing or fails, report "couldn't check" and never treat branches as gone (a failed SSH ls-remote once made a cleanup script delete a live worktree).
- **Output:** a short additional-context note, e.g. "12 stale worktrees (10 merged, 2 detached) in stare, citare; run /<skill> to clean up", plus the list in a file. Fast: cache the remote check for a few minutes, cap the work per session start.
- **Report-only by default.** Removal is a separate skill or command that the user or agent runs: remove only worktrees with an empty `git status --porcelain --ignore-submodules=none`, use `--force` only for a clean worktree that refuses because of submodules, delete the merged local branch, `git worktree prune`, and never touch a worktree with an open PR.
- Optionally the same check runs as a periodic sweep (systemd user timer) on machines where sessions are long-lived.

Fits next to forge-tracker's `/groom`, which already finds stale branches and worktrees on demand; the hook is the nudge that makes it run.
response.title: Hook: find stale git worktrees at session start and report them

Ruling D40 (2026-10-20): the "record blocking as native links" rule from [#92](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/pull/92) lived only in `commands/next.md` and `commands/groom.md`, so an agent filing or linking issues without running `/next` or `/groom` never read it. This adds a small `forge-tracker` skill that carries it.

**The skill** (`plugins/forge-tracker/skills/forge-tracker/SKILL.md`) triggers on:

> Use when filing an issue, recording that one issue blocks, waits on or depends on another, linking issues, or about to write "Blocked by", "Depends on" or "Blocks" in an issue body or comment. Records blocking as the forge's native links, which /next and /groom read, and labels person-only work when filing.

Its body says three things:

- Record blocking with `"${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT}/scripts/forge-tracker" link add <issue> --blocked-by <blocker>` and `link remove`, or, without the plugin, the `gh api` calls it makes (the blocker's id from `GET /issues/{n}`, then `POST`/`DELETE .../dependencies/blocked_by`). Never only as a sentence in a body or comment, since `/next` and `/groom` read only native links. Link only issues you filed or are working on, or when the user asks (the same limit `next.md` sets).
- Label person-only work at filing with the repo's `labels.needs_human` or `labels.decision` from `.claude/forge-tracker.local.md`; with neither configured, file it unlabelled and say so rather than guess a name.
- What `/next`, `/catchup` (with `--no-mark` when an agent runs it for itself) and `/groom` are for.

**No `allowed-tools`.** I left it out. The skill triggers whenever issues are filed or linked, so pre-approving `forge-tracker link *` would let an agent write links to a shared forge, on its own reading of what blocks what, with no prompt in any such session. The script's checks refuse stale or duplicate links, not wrong ones, and `/groom` catches prose blocking, not a mislink. The permission prompt is the one place the user sees a link before it lands; term-recorder's pre-approval covers a local, read-only capture, which is a different case.

**Docs.** The spec's working-rules section says the skill is built with these two rules and is the seed of phase 2, the blocking bullet no longer says "until the skill exists", a person-only labelling bullet joins the list, and phase 2 notes the seed. response.body:
**Root cause.** When a session has no stored record under its own id, `loadRecord()` falls back to `forkedFrom()`, which only looks for a parent when the session's task files hold decision items (`carried.length === 0` returned null). Ledger items never reach task files, so a session whose queue was all `decision_add` items looked brand new after the id changed: empty queue, counters at zero, and the next item reused D1. The engine passes no resumed-from or forked-from id in any hook input or `$.session` call, so the old id has to be inferred.

**Fix.** The conversation is what survives an id change, so the plugin now reads it with `$.session.messages()`:

- `hooks/lineage.ts` (new) builds a trail from the transcript: each ledger item `decision_add` and `decision_update` reported (label and every body it had), whether `decision_close` closed it, the ledger lines of the resume reminder, and every label the conversation used, TaskCreate ones included.
- `carriedFrom()` (was `forkedFrom()`) picks the most recently used `session:` record that agrees with every sign the session has: its ledger holds every trail item by label, at least one word for word, and is closed wherever the transcript closed it; when the session also has task files, the record's task list has to match them as before. With no sign at all it adopts nothing. An unrelated session in the same project never has the same tool answers in its transcript, so it is never taken; a stale record that still shows an item open which the conversation closed is skipped, so closed items aren't revived.
- `hydrate()` raises the counters to cover every label the transcript shows, so numbering never repeats a label even when no record is found (pruned, say).
- When session start finds no record and the transcript isn't loaded yet, the next `UserPromptSubmit` hydrates again.
- README: the sync section and the limits describe the transcript match; `--fork-session` now carries ledger items (not task-list ones).

**Tests.** `tests/lineage.test.ts` covers the trail parser and the match rule. `tests/register.test.tsx` adds seven cases: ledger-only carry-over (with numbering continuing at D2 and the old record left alone), a transcript loaded after session start (found by the resume hook, and by the next prompt without one), mixed task-list and ledger (a more recent sibling with the same task files but a different ledger is refused), no carry-over from an unrelated session that also starts at D1, an empty transcript adopting nothing, a closed item not revived from a stale record, and counter continuity from transcript labels alone. All seven fail against `main`'s hooks; `claude plugin test`: 110 pass. `claude plugin validate --strict` passes.

**On screen** (Claude Code 2.1.302, `--plugin-dir` copy, Haiku 5.5 without the task tools): a session created D1 with `decision_add`; `claude --resume <id> --fork-session` came back as a new session id, and `/decisions` listed `D1 … (ledger, waiting 0m)` with the footer showing 1 decision; the store held D1 under both ids. A harness restart or a background fork that changes the id wasn't reproduced on screen; those go through the same transcript path and are covered by the tests.

Closes #94

response.body:
## What happened

A session whose only queued items were fallback-ledger items (created with `decision_add` because the task tools were not available) lost all of them when the session was resumed under a new session id. `/decisions` then reported "No open decisions or actions" while the store file still held the item, status `pending`, under the old session key.

Observed on 2026-10-18 with session-decisions v2026.10.18.1, Claude Code 2.1.289:

- Session `84d4a7be-…` created `D1` via `decision_add` (TaskCreate was not in the tool list at the time).
- The harness restarted at 23:54:13 and continued the same conversation as session `9b715abc-…`.
- `/decisions` in the resumed session showed nothing. `~/.claude/plugins/store/session-decisions_*.json` still had `session:84d4a7be-…` with `counters.D = 1` and the D1 ledger item pending.
- The task tools became available in the resumed session, so the item had to be re-created by hand (and got the label D1 again, since the new session's counters started at zero).

## Why

`hooks/register.tsx`:

- `hydrate()` calls `loadRecord($, sid, fromFiles)` with the new session id. No record exists under `session:<new id>`.
- `loadRecord()` falls through to `forkedFrom($, sid, fromFiles ?? [])`.
- `forkedFrom()` returns `null` on its first line when `carried.length === 0`. `carried` is built from the task files only; ledger items are never in task files. So a session with ledger-only items is indistinguishable from a brand-new session and starts empty.
- `/decisions` reads the in-memory `items` atom, which `hydrate()` just left empty, rather than consulting the store.

Any resume (or fork) of a session that has ledger items but no task-list items hits this.

## Possible fixes

- If the harness passes the resumed-from session id on `session.start` (or anywhere in the hook input), use it directly in `loadRecord()` before falling back to `forkedFrom()`.
- Otherwise, when a session has no record and no task files, adopt the most recently touched `session:` record whose ledger has open items and whose transcript lives in the same project directory, and migrate it to the new key. The existing "word for word" match can't apply, since there are no task files to compare, so a recency-plus-project heuristic is the available signal.
- Either way, `/decisions` could print a one-line hint when the store holds open ledger items under a different session key than the current one, so the loss is at least visible.

## Repro

1. In a session where TaskCreate is not offered, create an item with `decision_add`.
2. Resume the session under a new id (background it, or restart the harness so it resumes).
3. Run `/decisions`.
response.title: session-decisions: ledger-only items are lost when a session resumes under a new id

- What exists today: transcript view (ctrl+o), the session JSONL under `~/.claude/projects/`, `/resume`, terminal scrollback and tmux copy-mode search, any statusline or hook APIs that could help.

`[more]` opened Claude Code's question dialog (`$.ui.ask`), which can't scroll, so the plugin cut the description to the screen and ended it with `… N more lines not shown`. Anything below that was unreachable.

## What changed

`[more]`, or a press on the card's label, now shows the item in full in the plugin's own queue pane, in place of the list. A `Pane` body is a scrollable window in the function-hooks API (`Pane.scroll: SiteScroll`; `ui.scroll` moves it by a row per arrow, `bodyRows` per page key, `contentRows` for Home/End, and with the wheel), so the view draws the whole item and Claude Code does the scrolling. No paging was needed.

- Top row: kind chip, label, `recommends` tag, a dim `↑↓ PgUp PgDn scroll · Esc closes` hint, age.
- Actions next, so they're reachable at any scroll offset (Tab walks them too): **Accept** or **Done**, **Answer**, **Copy link**, **Copy `<command>`**, and **Back** (or **Close** when the pane opened just for this item).
- Then the question, `Link:`, `Recommended: <whole recommendation>`, and the description, drawn as markdown (lists, tables, fences), ending in a dim `─ end of D3 ─` line, so you can tell you've reached the end.
- From a transcript card, the pane opens for the item, with the keys, at any width. Accept, Done and Answer fill the prompt and close it again. From the open queue, they go back to the list. The open is issued before anything else is awaited: in my first run the plugin awaited `$.ui.panes()` first, and Claude Code then treated the open as unasked and refused it below 110 columns.
- Closing the pane while it shows an item forgets the item and doesn't count as dismissing the sidebar.
- The dialog-fitting code (`dialogQuestion`, `fitRows`, `wrappedRows`) is gone. `dialogExtras` and `dialogText` are renamed `detailsExtras` and `descriptionText`.

response.body:
The details pane that opens from **more** cannot be scrolled, so anything taller than the pane is unreachable.

### What happens

A decision item created with a long `description` renders into the pane. Once the text exceeds the pane's height, the overflow is simply cut — no scrollbar, no keyboard scrolling, no way to reach the rest.

### Why it bites

The session-decisions skill explicitly tells the agent to put everything the user needs in the description:

> Keep the subject to one short line: the question, the recommendation and the link. Everything else goes in the description

and

> The user reads it in a dialog that keeps your line breaks but shows no markdown and cuts what doesn't fit the screen, so put what they need to decide first.

So the skill already knows the pane truncates and compensates by ordering content. But "put the important part first" only works when the rest is *optional*. A decision with measured evidence — several numbered findings, a table of counts, the risk in both directions — does not compress into a screenful, and the parts that get cut are exactly the ones that justify the recommendation.

Observed on a decision whose description carried per-partition row counts and a probe result with controls; the probe result, which was the whole basis for the recommendation, was below the fold and unreachable.

### Expected

Scrollable with the keyboard at minimum (arrows / page keys), ideally mouse wheel too. A visible affordance that there *is* more would help — right now truncation is indistinguishable from the agent having written a short description.

Agents were writing blocking into issue bodies (`Blocked by: #17`, `Blocks #18`), which `/next` and `/groom` can't see: they read only GitHub's native relationship graph. This adds a way to write that graph, a `/groom` check that finds the prose, and the rule in the text agents read.

**Writes.** Two new operations, `link-add` and `link-remove`, take `issue`, `blocker` and (for a blocker in another project) `blocker_project`. On GitHub they're `POST /repos/{o}/{r}/issues/{n}/dependencies/blocked_by` with `{"issue_id": <blocker's id>}` and `DELETE .../dependencies/blocked_by/{id}`, both under the repo's own REST path. A self-link fails validation; then, before anything is sent and before the write-wrapper too, they read the issue's current blockers and refuse an add whose link already exists or a remove whose link doesn't, and an add whose either side is a pull request or closed. They're logged like every other write. `forge-tracker link add 18 --blocked-by 17` (or `--blocked-by owner/repo#17`) and `link remove` run them from arguments; `forge-tracker write link-add` takes JSON. `unlink` stays the `/groom` fix that removes a link only once its blocker has closed.

**`/groom`.** A new check, "blocking written only as prose", reads open issue bodies for `Blocked by: #N`, `blocked on #N`, `Depends on #N` and, only where a line starts, `Blocks #N` or `Blocking: #N` (each with a list of `#N` or `owner/repo#N`). Code blocks and spans, quoted lines, HTML comments, struck-out text, negations and self-references don't count. A sentence with a native link behind it is left alone. Otherwise:

- an open blocker is a `link-add` proposal (`link-add #18 blocked by #17`), applied through `groom apply` like every other fix;
- a closed blocker is listed for you as stale prose (only a person edits a body);
- a pull request named as a blocker, a blocked issue in another project, or a blocker that couldn't be read is unclear.

It never edits a body. A blocker that isn't an open or recently closed issue here is read once by number (`GET /repos/{o}/{r}/issues/{n}`); no existing read query changed, so the recorded fixtures still replay unchanged.

**Working rule.** `commands/next.md` and `commands/groom.md` now tell agents to record blocking with `forge-tracker link add` (or the `gh api` call it makes) and never only as prose, since `/next` sees only native links. The spec's working rules gain the same bullet. Nothing else in the repo told agents to write `Blocked by` prose; I grepped for it.

Sub-issues aren't included: they're a parent and child relationship, not blocking, and `/next` doesn't read them as blocking.

Closes #91
response.title: feat(forge-tracker): record blocking as native links and find prose blocking in /groom

response.body:
Agents are writing blocking relationships into issue **bodies** as prose — `Blocked by: #17`, `Blocks #18` — instead of using GitHub's native relationship metadata.

### Why that is worse than it looks

The prose form is invisible to everything that reads structure:

- GitHub's own UI shows no blocked/blocking state, so the board is wrong.
- `forge-tracker next` classifies items as `agent-ready`, `blocked` or `unknown` **from the relationship graph**. An item blocked only in prose classifies as agent-ready, and the report then recommends starting work that cannot start.
- `/groom` fixes "blocked labels with nothing linked" and "links to closed blockers". Neither can see a sentence.
- Closing the blocker does not update the blocked issue, so the prose goes stale silently and nobody notices.

In a session today, several issues carried `Blocked by: #17` in the body while `forge-tracker next` reported `Blocked: nothing blocked`. Both were "right" — the tracker read the graph, which was empty.

### What it should do

Use the GitHub relationship features — sub-issues, or the `blocked_by` / `blocks` relationships exposed through the API and the issue UI — so the graph is populated and `forge-tracker` reads real state.

Prose may stay as a human-readable gloss, but it must not be the only record.

### Where the guidance belongs

The skills that tell an agent to file issues should say this explicitly. Right now nothing instructs otherwise, so an agent reaches for the obvious thing and writes a sentence. A short rule — *blocking relationships go in the relationship metadata, never only in the body* — plus the API call to set one, would fix it at the source.
response.title: Issues record blocking in the body text instead of GitHub's relationship metadata

response.body:
Ruling D37: repos released with yeet keep GitHub's default merge commit subject ("Merge pull request #N from <branch>"), which yeet skips, so only a PR's own Conventional Commits release. Until now this repo's merge commits took the PR title, and yeet counted them too; forge-tracker 2026.10.18.1's CHANGELOG lists "#80 …" and "#81 …" beside each PR's own commits.

- forge-release skill (`SKILL.md`, `references/yeet-setup.md`, `references/troubleshooting.md`, `templates/release-check.sh`): setup recommends merge commits with the default message (`merge_commit_title=MERGE_MESSAGE`, `merge_commit_message=PR_TITLE`) and squash and rebase off, with the web UI path and a `gh api` command; repos managed as code set it there (Pulumi `github.Repository` `allow_merge_commit`, `merge_commit_title`, `merge_commit_message`, `allow_squash_merge`, `allow_rebase_merge`; Terraform `github_repository` uses the same names). Troubleshooting covers every PR listed twice when the merge subject is the PR title. `pr-title.yml` is now optional, only for repos that keep PR-title merge subjects.
- `.github/scripts/release-check.sh`: the comment says yeet skips a merge commit only when its subject is the default one.
- `AGENTS.md`: the Versioning notes describe the default merge subject, and a releasable PR needs a releasing commit, not a releasing title.

This PR doesn't change the repo settings, which still read `merge_commit_title=PR_TITLE`, `merge_commit_message=PR_BODY`, `allow_squash_merge=true`. Until they change to `MERGE_MESSAGE`/`PR_TITLE` with squash off, the AGENTS.md text describes the target state, and merging this PR under the current setting adds one more PR-title line to the next forge-release changelog entry.

response.body:
Follow-up from [lokkju/infra#284](https://github.com/lokkju/infra/issues/284) (plan: docs/plans/2026-10-16-claude-delegation-and-cattle.md in lokkju/infra, Part 1, D4). The plan puts the measurement script here because it reads transcripts for every project, not one repo.

Spec:

- A `uv run` script, standard library only. Arguments: a project directory under `~/.claude/projects/` (or a cwd to derive it from: non-alphanumerics become `-`) and a date range.
- Input: each `<session id>.jsonl` in the project directory whose records fall in the range, plus `<session id>/subagents/agent-<id>.jsonl` and its `.meta.json` (agent type, model, description).
- Walk the non-sidechain records (`isSidechain` false) in order. A prompt is a `type: user` record whose `message.content` is a string, excluding injected strings (`<task-notification>`, `<system-reminder>`, `<local-command...>`). Tool results (list content) are not prompts.
- `type: assistant` records carry `message.id`, `message.content[]` (with `tool_use` blocks naming the tool) and `message.usage`. One API response is several records with the same `message.id`; dedupe on it before summing usage.
- "Reads" are Bash, Read, Grep, Glob, WebFetch and WebSearch calls. A run of reads ends at a prompt or an Agent (or Task) call.
- Context per call is `input_tokens + cache_read_input_tokens + cache_creation_input_tokens`.
- Per prompt: tool calls by name, whether any was Agent, the longest run of reads, peak main-thread context. Skip prompts with no tool calls.
- Per session: prompts with tool calls, share with an Agent call, longest read run, number of runs of 10 or more reads, median and peak main-thread context, and the subagents' summed tokens from `subagents/*.jsonl`.
- Output: a table (and `--json`). Numbers only; it never prints prompt, tool input or result content.
- The transcript format is internal and changes between Claude Code versions; fail loudly on a record shape it doesn't recognize instead of guessing.

Use: a baseline over the two weeks before the infra hook (`.claude/hooks/read-nudge.py`, project scope, N = 8) went in, then a rerun two weeks after, compared on share of prompts with an Agent call, runs of 10+ reads, and median main-thread context. The baseline numbers in the plan's table were done by hand with `jq` over sessions `b54339de` and `3eb3b414`. If the numbers move, the hook moves here too and goes to user scope.
response.title: Transcript measurement script for Claude Code delegation

response.body:
Adds `scripts/delegation-stats.py`, the measurement script from #77 (Part 1, D4 of the lokkju/infra#284 plan): a standard-library `uv run` script with a PEP 723 header and no dependencies.

```bash
uv run scripts/delegation-stats.py ~/projects/infra --since 2026-10-01 --until 2026-10-14 [--session ID-PREFIX ...] [--json]
```

The project argument is a directory under `~/.claude/projects/`, its name, or a cwd mapped to it (non-alphanumerics become `-`). Dates are UTC and inclusive; a prompt is in range when its own timestamp is, and a subagent when its first record is. It walks the non-sidechain records, dedupes assistant records on `message.id` (tool calls on `tool_use.id`), counts Bash, Read, Grep, Glob, WebFetch and WebSearch as reads, ends a run at a prompt or an Agent/Task call, and takes context per API call as input + cache_read + cache_creation tokens. It prints a row per session plus an `all` row, or JSON with the per-prompt numbers and per-subagent token sums (agent type and model from `.meta.json`; the description is never read out). An unknown record type, content block, or missing `message.id` or usage field exits 2 with `file:line` and the key name, never the content.

One choice beyond the issue's text: user strings flagged `isMeta`, `isCompactSummary` or `isVisibleInTranscriptOnly` count as injected too, along with the three prefixes. In these transcripts the `isMeta` strings are almost all messages from peer agents (`origin.kind: peer`), not anything typed.

CI: a new `scripts` job runs ruff check, ruff format --check and `scripts/tests` on Python 3.11 and 3.14. The tests (17) use synthetic transcripts only and cover dedupe, read runs and their terminators, injected-string exclusion, sidechain exclusion, subagent token sums, date-range filtering, cwd mapping, the session filter and the fail-loudly paths.

## Baseline comparison

I ran it read-only over `~/.claude/projects/-home-lokkju-projects-infra/` for the plan's two sessions, and over all 45 projects on this machine, which all parse.

| Session | Source | Prompts with tool calls | ...with an Agent call | Longest read run | Runs of 10+ | Context median / max |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `b54339de` | plan (hand, `jq`) | 266 | 77 (29%) | 74 | 42 | 416k / 870k |
| `b54339de` | script, prefixes only | 266 | 77 (29%) | 74 | 43 | 416k / 870k |
| `b54339de` | script, as shipped | 167 | 52 (31%) | 74 | 46 | 416k / 870k |
| `3eb3b414` | plan (hand, `jq`) | 157 | 39 (25%) | 33 | 17 | 442k / 908k |
| `3eb3b414` | script, prefixes only | 157 | 39 (25%) | 34 | 18 | 442k / 908k |
| `3eb3b414` | script, as shipped | 114 | 37 (32%) | 36 | 19 | 443k / 908k |

Subagents, as shipped: `b54339de` 112 subagents, 693.8M tokens; `3eb3b414` 72 subagents, 352.4M tokens.

With only the issue's three prefixes excluded, prompts and Agent counts match the hand count exactly and context matches. The read runs differ by one (one more run of 10+ in both sessions, and a longest run one longer in `3eb3b414`) because the hand count ended runs at every user string, including task notifications; with no exclusion at all the script gives exactly 74/42 and 33/17. As shipped, `isMeta` peer messages no longer start prompts, so their tool calls join the human prompt before them: 99 and 43 fewer prompts with tool calls, slightly longer runs, and a higher Agent share. The 1k median difference on `3eb3b414` is one API call (1,065 against 1,066), a response to a peer message that arrived before the first human prompt and so has no prompt to belong to. The Phase 1 comparison should rerun the baseline with the script rather than reuse the hand numbers.

Closes #77

More leaves the action row. A dim `[more]` now ends the card's text (the question, or the recommendation qualifier when there is one) and opens the same question dialog More did. The item label still opens it. The action row keeps Accept, Done, Answer and the short link.

## When `[more]` shows

`hasMore` in `hooks/more.ts` decides, and it's tested directly. It's true when the dialog shows something the card doesn't:

- a description (anything `dialogText` keeps; whitespace alone doesn't count);
- a recommendation the card cuts short. With today's `shortRecommendation` a cut choice puts the whole recommendation on the qualifier line, so this never fires yet, but it's checked;
- a link the dialog spells out as a URL and offers to copy: a URL token (drawn on its own line), or a short reference the session's forge resolves;
- a code span in the question or description, which the dialog offers to copy.

I made one call against the issue's wording: a long reference no forge resolves (`gitlab/group/proj#4`) is drawn on its own line, but the dialog has nothing more for it (no `Link:` line, no Copy link), so it gets no `[more]`. `popup()` now reads the URL and command from the same `dialogExtras`, so the card and the dialog can't drift apart.

## Placement

Claude Code refuses a `Button` inside a `Text` ("Button inside an inline element"), so `[more]` can't flow inline in the text. `moreSplit` works out where the text wraps for the card's width (the pane's `bodyColumns`, or the viewport's columns for transcript cards, less the frame) and splits the markdown into the rows above and the last row. The card then draws the last row with `[more]` beside it. When the last row has no room, or when the drawn width can't be told from the text (a link, non-ASCII, a word longer than a row, an emphasis span across the split, an unknown width), `[more]` goes on a row of its own. If the width is off, the rows just break somewhere else; `[more]` is never drawn over the text.

response.body:
On an open card, More sits in the button row (`[ Accept ] [ Answer ] [ More ]`) and always shows. `register.tsx` on main renders it unconditionally, even when the dialog would add nothing the card doesn't already show. That costs a button slot on every card, and it hides the one signal that matters: whether this item has more to read.

What I'd like instead:

- **Inline, after the text.** Put `[more]` at the end of the card's question text (or after the recommendation qualifier, when that's the last line shown), as a dim inline link or button rather than a row button. It reads as "this continues". Clicking it opens the same question dialog More opens today, and the item label keeps opening it too.
- **Only when there's more.** Show it only when the dialog would show something the card doesn't:
  - the item has a non-empty description;
  - the recommendation is shortened on the card (the full recommendation differs from the chip or qualifier shown);
  - the link is long enough to be drawn on its own line, or is resolved to a URL the card doesn't show;
  - code spans the dialog offers to copy.
  
  When none of these holds, there's no `[more]`, and the card's text is the whole item.
- **The button row keeps** only Accept, Done and Answer, and the short link at the end.

Check it on screen with term-recorder at 100x30 and 60x30, for an item with a description and one without. Cover the inline placement (wrapping onto the last line, or onto its own line when the text fills the width) and the absence of `[more]` on the bare item. The pane cards and the transcript cards should behave the same way.

response.body:
Two `/next` changes, one commit each.

**Untagged items in labelled repos ([#83](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/83)).** The slate's `person_only` map now accepts, with a reason, any item that isn't blocked and has no person-only or agent label, in labelled repos too, not only `unclassified` ones. A labelled item stays as its label says: an item with the agent label is refused in the queue, and a needs-human or decision item is in the queue already. The report shows it as `judged person-only: <reason>`. Without a slate, an agent-ready item with no agent label is marked `untagged` in the text report (with a count line) and carries `untagged: true` in `--json`, so a reader of the CLI run, `--json` or an agent's own run can tell the default from a judgement. `commands/next.md` tells the assistant to read untagged items' bodies when ranking, queue the ones needing the owner with a reason, and suggest tagging them.

**An evaluated recommendation ([#78](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/78)).** The slate gains a `recommend` section that `save-slate` validates against the facts and the rest of the slate:

- `merge`: open PRs ready to merge (not a draft, `conflicts: no`, CI `success`, review approved or not required); `conflicts: unknown` is refused.
- `you`: one pick from the slate's queue, then at most two more.
- `start` / `wait`: every lane once, by letter or number, each with a reason; `start` stays within `agent_cap` when it's given.
- `not_yet`: open issues or PRs to leave for now; none can also be picked, started or merged.

The report closes with a `Recommended next` block that says it's Claude's judgement and that nothing starts or merges until the user says so; `--json` carries it as `slate.recommend`. `commands/next.md` says how to judge impact. `/next` stays read-only.

README and spec updated. The golden replay fixture is unchanged: its config labels nothing, so no item is agent-ready there.

Closes #83
Closes #78

response.body:
When a repo has its labels configured (for example `needs_human: needs-human`, `decision: question`), every open, unblocked issue without one of those labels counts as **agent-ready** by default. The `unclassified` state from [#80](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/pull/80) applies only to repos with no labels configured. The slate's `person_only` map, which moves an item into the user's queue with a stated reason, accepts unclassified items only.

So in a labelled repo, an untagged issue that only the owner can act on lands in the agent lanes, and the slate can't move it. On lokkju/skills, #10 ("standardize on yeet …?", a decision) showed as agent-ready until it was hand-tagged `question`.

**1. Let the slate move untagged items in labelled repos too.**
- `save-slate` should accept a `person_only` entry, with its reason, for any item with no person-only label and no blocking, not only unclassified ones.
- A labelled item stays as its label says: a needs-human or decision item is already in the queue, and an `agent-ready` item can't be moved out of the lanes this way.
- The report shows it as `judged person-only: <reason>`, as it does for unclassified items today.
- `commands/next.md` tells the assistant to read the untagged items' bodies when ranking. Ones that need the owner (a decision, physical work, a device or test window, an external event, parked) go in the queue with a reason, and the assistant suggests tagging them so the next run doesn't depend on judgement.

**2. Without a slate, don't present untagged items as settled agent work.**
- The report and `--json` should separate untagged items from labelled ones in labelled repos. That could be an `untagged` mark, or a separate sub-list under Agent-ready.
- This covers a report read before any slate is saved: the CLI run directly, `--json`, or an agent running /next for its own purposes. A reader then sees that "agent-ready" for those items is the default, not a judgement.
- The `/next` command always builds a slate when the report says `slate: needed`, so in normal use part 1 covers it. This part is for the other paths.

Tests: a labelled repo with an untagged decision-shaped issue. `save-slate` accepts it in the queue with a reason and refuses it without one. A tagged `agent-ready` item is refused in the queue. The no-slate report marks untagged items.

Related: [#69](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/69), [#78](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/78).
response.title: forge-tracker: /next lets the slate move untagged items into your queue in labelled repos, and marks them untagged without a slate

response.body:
`/next` ranks and groups, but it doesn't recommend. The slate gives you a queue and a set of agent lanes, then stops. The reader still has to work out which one thing to do first and why, and on a repo with five lanes that's the question `/next` exists to answer.

`/next` should end with an evaluated recommendation:

- **One pick for the user, with its reason.** For example: "Decide #10 first: it unblocks the forge-release skill (#11), and nothing else in your queue unblocks agent work." Then the next one or two items after it, if they matter.
- **Which lanes to start now, and how many.** These go up to the session's agent cap, picked by impact and readiness: what each unblocks, its tier and due date, whether it's a bug or a feature, how settled its design is (spec ruled vs open questions), how close it is to merged work that's still fresh, and the risk of conflicting with other in-flight PRs. Each pick gets a one-line reason, and a lane being skipped gets one too ("#19 waits: research with no design yet").
- **What's ready to merge.** Open PRs with CI green, no conflicts, and an approved review where one is required, including bot PRs like Dependabot's. They're listed as a merge-first step, since they're the cheapest progress available. A PR with `conflicts: unknown` is never ready.
- **What it would not do yet,** and why: umbrella issues, items waiting on a decision, and drift that `/groom` should fix first.

How it fits the design:

- The script can't judge any of this; the slate step can, as it already does for lanes. So the slate gains a `recommend` section, made of picks with reasons, that `save-slate` validates. Every pick must refer to an item in the facts or an open PR, in its right class.
- The report prints it as a closing "Recommended next" block, and `commands/next.md` tells the assistant to write it from the facts and to say plainly that it's a judgement.
- `/next` stays read-only. A recommendation is never an action, so the assistant still asks before starting a lane or merging anything.
- `--json` includes the recommendation.

Related: [#24](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/24) (the original /next), [#69](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/69) (unlabeled repos).
response.title: forge-tracker: /next should end with an evaluated recommendation, not just lanes

Writes the forge-release skill: a decision tree first, then setup, migration, troubleshooting and release-triggered deploys, each with a reference file, plus templates to copy into a repo.

## Decision tree

- **Default: yeet**, for SemVer and CalVer, single package or monorepo, on GitHub, GitLab and Azure DevOps (the [lokkju/skills#10](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/10) ruling of 2026-10-18).
- **Cargo packages: release-plz.** It publishes to crates.io and runs cargo-semver-checks, which yeet doesn't, and `Cargo.lock` records the package's own version, which yeet can't rewrite (the same defect the dbxdebug pilot found in `uv.lock`, with no hatch-vcs equivalent for Cargo).
- **Forgejo, Gitea, Codeberg, Bitbucket:** yeet doesn't support them, so the skill stops and asks. I didn't name a tool there, since I have no evidence for one.
- Repos on release-please today move when someone is working in them anyway (the #10 proposal the 2026-10-14 ruling accepted).
- Versioning: SemVer for things others depend on, CalVer `YYYY.0M.0D.MICRO` in UTC for snapshots.

## What it settles from the #11 brainstorm

- release-please gets no setup reference of its own after the ruling; it appears only as a migration source (config and marker mapping, `pre_major_features_bump_patch: false` for its pre-1.0 behaviour, moving the publish job to `release: published`).
- uv projects must take their version from the tag (hatch-vcs), from the pilot's `uv.lock` finding.
- The App credentials default to `YEET_APP_ID` (variable) and `YEET_APP_PRIVATE_KEY` (secret), the names `github-app-create --to github` stores and yeet's docs use. One App per owner; repos are added in the App's settings because a gh OAuth token gets 403.
- yeet runs from the release tarball pinned by SHA-256 (no Docker daemon needed), telemetry off in config and `DO_NOT_TRACK=1`. The templates pin v0.17.0, the version this repo and dbxdebug run; v0.17.1 is out.
- Deploy guards in `templates/deploy.yml`: release-shaped tags only, the tag on main, the newest release tag only, a concurrency group no other workflow shares, and nothing created. A `workflow_dispatch` with a tag input is the recovery path.
- Every lesson in #11's list is in a reference: the dry-run HEAD requirement and its workarounds, bare first-of-day CalVer tags, the webhook-less manifest (through `github-app-create`), the classic-token 403, telemetry, `GITHUB_URL` on GARM, `XDG_CACHE_HOME`, the private-repo `gh auth git-credential` fetch, and the shared concurrency group.

The templates for `release-check.sh` and `release-check.yml` come from the dbxdebug pilot (the version that handles a target path of `.`), with the comments made generic. `templates/` follows the structure #11 decided on.

## Open questions

- **Merge commit title.** This repo's merge commits take the PR title, and yeet reads them as commits: the forge-tracker 2026.10.18.1 changelog lists "classify unlabelled repos honestly ... (#80)" alongside each of that PR's own commits. The skill documents both settings (the PR title adds one line per PR and needs `pr-title.yml`; GitHub's default "Merge pull request #N" subject is skipped) and doesn't pick one. Should new repos keep the PR title, or switch to the default message so each change is listed once? Also: should squash be turned off on repos that standardize on merge commits?
- **The SemVer pilot hasn't released yet.** [lokkju/dbxdebug#26](https://github.com/lokkju/dbxdebug/pull/26) merged, but dbxdebug's newest release is still v0.5.0 from release-please, so the SemVer path (bump, tag, `release: published` to PyPI) hasn't run end to end under yeet. #10 asked for the pilot before the skill made yeet the SemVer default; the 2026-10-18 ruling makes it the default regardless.
- **GitLab and Azure DevOps** get the `.yeet.yaml`, token and permission notes and a pointer to yeet's pipeline examples, but no templates and no release-check equivalent. Templates for them can wait for a repo that needs them.

Closes #11

_Moved from my private repo, where it was skills-marketplace#8._

The forge-release plugin has the `github-app-create` script (0.3.0: `--port`, `--no-browser`, `--to sops`) and no skill yet. Brainstorming got this far, and the next step is presenting the design in sections, then the spec in `docs/specs/`, then the plan.

## Decided (2026-10-04)

- **Scope:** setting a repo up, migrating a repo from another release flow, troubleshooting, and the deploy workflow a release triggers, with its guards. Channel promotion is tracked separately.
- **Structure:** one `SKILL.md` with the decision tree and flow, `references/` per topic (yeet, release-please, release-plz, deploy workflow, migration, troubleshooting), and `templates/` made generic from a working migration's files (`yeet.yml`, `.yeet.yaml`, the deploy guards). Shareable: no personal repos, paths or names.
- **Decision tree:** yeet for CalVer and for anything on GitLab or Azure DevOps, release-please for SemVer packages on GitHub, release-plz for Rust crates, pending #10 (standardize on yeet).

## Lessons to carry in

- yeet's `--dry-run` needs local HEAD to equal the release branch's remote head; a scratch `--config` copy with `branch:` changed works around it.
- A bare first-of-day tag (`vYYYY.MM.DD`) is invisible to yeet; retag it `.1`.
- yeet needs a GitHub App token for its release to start other workflows; `github-app-create` must not send `hook_attributes` without a URL, and adding repos to an installation needs a classic token (a gh OAuth token gets 403), so repo access is set in the App's settings.
- Telemetry is on by default: `telemetry.enabled: false` and `DO_NOT_TRACK=1`.
- Self-hosted runners:
  - Without a Docker daemon, run yeet from its release tarball checked against a pinned SHA-256 instead of `docker://`.
  - Runners that export `GITHUB_URL` (GARM does) make yeet call `/api/v3/...` as if on GitHub Enterprise; set `GITHUB_URL: ""` in the yeet step.
  - Cache paths follow `XDG_CACHE_HOME`, which may not be `~/.cache`.
- Private repos fetching fresh tags in a deploy need `git -c credential.helper='!gh auth git-credential'`.
- Deploy guards: deploy only from main, only the newest release tag, and create nothing (no tags, no releases) in the deploy workflow. Filter "newest tag" to the release shape so a stray `v*` tag can't block deploys.
- A shared deploy concurrency group can cancel a queued run.
