response.body:
_Moved from my private repo, where it was skills-marketplace#6._

The forge-release skill's decision tree currently routes CalVer (and anything on GitLab or Azure DevOps) to yeet, SemVer packages on GitHub to release-please, and Rust crates to release-plz. The question is whether the middle branch should go to yeet too, so one tool covers every non-crate repo. The python-project skill's release-please default would follow whatever this decides.

## The case for keeping release-please, checked

- **Native version files.** Weaker than it sounds. Neither tool updates `uv.lock`: release-please has googleapis/release-please#2561 open for it. yeet updates `pyproject.toml` through a marker comment (`version = "1.2.3" # x-yeet-version`) and `package.json` through `json_pointer: /version`, which covers the files these repos publish from.
- **Tokens.** No difference. Both run on `GITHUB_TOKEN` when the publish step lives in the release workflow, and both need a GitHub App token only when the release has to start another workflow (one of my sites' deploy does).
- **Maturity.** The real one. yeet (monkescience/yeet, MIT) was created in February 2026 and has 4 contributors and 7 stars; release-please is Google's and widely used.
- **Language plugins.** release-please has strategies and plugins for Java, Ruby, PHP, Helm and node or cargo workspaces. None of these repos use them.

## Why the maturity risk is small here

- yeet runs as a container pinned by digest, so an abandoned yeet keeps working at the pinned version.
- Its only state is git tags and `CHANGELOG.md`, both tool-agnostic, so leaving it is a config swap. yeet's docs carry a migrate-from-release-please guide, and the reverse is the same shape.
- Telemetry is on by default; the skill already sets `telemetry.enabled: false` and `DO_NOT_TRACK=1`.

## What standardizing gets

One tool, one `.yeet.yaml` shape and one App pattern across GitHub, GitLab and Azure DevOps, for CalVer and SemVer. The skill's decision tree drops a branch, and its references drop the release-please setup and troubleshooting.

## Proposal

- New repos: yeet, SemVer or CalVer.
- Rust crates: release-plz stays. It publishes to crates.io and runs cargo-semver-checks, which yeet doesn't.
- Repos on release-please today move only when someone is in them anyway: lokkju/dbxdebug, lokkju/git-spreader and two private repos. release-plz today: lokkju/neovision and two private repos.
- python-project switches its release default to yeet.

## Not yet checked

- How yeet handles a Python package whose `uv.lock` records the project's own version (a release PR that bumps `pyproject.toml` but not `uv.lock` would fail `uv sync --locked`). release-please has the same gap; the usual fixes are a dynamic version (hatch-vcs) or a follow-up `uv lock` commit on the release branch.
- yeet's monorepo targets against release-please's linked versions, if a multi-package repo ever needs them.

response.body:
Two forge-tracker setup gaps: `/next` on a repo without person-only labels, and creating the labels setup finds missing.

### Unlabelled repos ([#69](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/69))

With neither `labels.needs_human` nor `labels.decision` configured (missing or `~`), an open issue that isn't blocked and matches no `person_only_markers` word is now `unclassified`, not `agent-ready`. The report's second line says how many there are, they're listed under "Not classified", and the empty queue says they may still need you. On lokkju/skills' recorded run, the 15 issues that used to come out agent-ready now show as unclassified (golden file updated).

The slate places them. A new `person_only` map (`{ref: reason}`) puts an unclassified item in the queue with the reason the assistant read in its text, and the report shows it as `judged person-only: <reason>`. An unclassified item can also go in a lane, and one the slate leaves out is listed as not placed. `save-slate` refuses a `person_only` entry for any item that isn't unclassified, one with no reason, or one missing from the queue, and it refuses an unclassified item in the queue that has no `person_only` entry. Repos with either label configured classify exactly as before; the existing slate tests pass unchanged.

`commands/next.md` tells the assistant to read each unclassified body and decide (physical work, a device or test window, research waiting on a decision, an external event, parked), and to say when its judgement put an item in the queue. An empty Blocked section now says `no blocking links recorded` rather than `nothing blocked`.

### Creating missing labels ([#76](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/76))

- `label-create` write operation: it checks name (at most 50 characters, no outer spaces), color (six hex digits) and description (at most 100) before anything goes out, then sends one POST to `/repos/{o}/{r}/labels` through the write transport, logs the result, and goes through `write_wrapper` when one is set. It reads the repo's labels first and refuses a name that exists in any case, with or without a wrapper.
- `forge-tracker labels create <names>`: each name is a default name (`needs-human`), a role (`needs_human`) or `role=name`. It refuses the whole list, writing nothing, when there are no names, the config already maps the role, a role or name appears twice, or the repo already has the name. Then it creates each label and prints the `labels.<role>: <name>` lines that replace the `~` (`--json` prints the same data). `--record` is refused for it, as for the other writes.
- `labels suggest` now lists the labels it would create, with a fixed color per role (needs-human d93f0b, decision fbca04, decided 0e8a16, blocked b60205, agent-ready 1d76db), as a `labels create` line and as `gh label create` commands.
- `/next` and `/catchup` ask a second, separate question after the config is accepted and run `labels create` only on an explicit yes, with exactly the approved names.

Tests run against the fake transport, with and without a wrapper, and cover a wrapper refusal, every refusal case, and a test that nothing is created without approved names (setup only sends GETs). The spec and the plugin README are updated.

The `cli.py` change is limited to the `labels create` subcommand and the label reader passed to the writer.

Closes #69
Closes #76

response.body:
Creating labels isn't one of forge-tracker's write operations, so first-use setup stops halfway. `forge-tracker labels suggest` ([#62](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/pull/62)) maps a repo's existing labels to the roles forge-tracker needs: needs-human, decision, decision-made, blocked and agent. It sets each role with no matching label to `~` and prints a `gh label create` command for the user to run. On lokkju/skills, for example, only `question` matched, so four of the five roles stay unset until someone runs four commands by hand and edits `.claude/forge-tracker.local.md` to replace each `~`.

Add label creation to the write layer `/groom` introduced ([#72](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/pull/72), `scripts/forge_tracker/writes.py`):

- **A `label-create` write operation:** name, color and description. It goes through the same rules as the other writes: validated before sending, POST only under the repo's own REST path, logged, and routed through `write_wrapper` when one is configured (D18). It refuses a name that already exists, compared without regard to case, since GitHub treats label names case-insensitively.
- **Setup uses it on approval:** after the user says yes to the proposed config, the `/catchup` and `/next` command text offers to create the missing labels too. Only on a second, explicit yes does it run `forge-tracker labels create` with the approved names, and then it writes those names into the config file in place of their `~`. Declining leaves the `gh label create` commands as they are today.
- **Defaults:** the names and descriptions `labels suggest` already prints (`needs-human`, `decided`, `blocked`, `agent-ready`), with a fixed color per role. `--json` reports what was created.
- **Tests:** against the fake transport, with and without the wrapper. A test checks that nothing is created without the approval step.

GitHub comes first, like the rest of the plugin. GitLab and Forgejo follow with [#21](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/21).

Related: [#59](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/59), [#69](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/69).

Two forge-tracker issues, one per commit, plus the gap [#75](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/75) found in "Waiting on you".

**Per-clone `tracker.web` and `tracker.forge` ([#71](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/71)).** forge-tracker now reads the git config keys session-decisions reads ([#70](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/pull/70)), with `git config --get`:

- `tracker.web` (an https repo URL) replaces the origin remote's host and path, so a clone whose remote is an SSH alias, a mirror or a push-only URL reads the right repo, and a clone with no `origin` works too. The path is split as session-decisions splits it (the whole path on GitLab, the last two segments elsewhere).
- The kind is `tracker.forge` (github, gitlab, forgejo, or gitea read as forgejo), else `forge:` in `.claude/forge-tracker.local.md`, else the built-in host rules. `forge:` is documented as the per-repo default, committed or not, and `tracker.forge` as the per-clone override that wins over it.
- `api_base:` and `ca_file:` still come only from the config file.
- A value forge-tracker can't use stops the command with the key named, rather than falling back to the remote it was meant to replace.

**Catchup across a folder of repos ([#75](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/75)).** Started in a folder that isn't a git repo but holds several, `catchup` used to exit 2. It now reads each repo and prints one report:

- The repos are `--workspace DIR`, else `repos:` in the folder's own `.claude/forge-tracker.local.md` (the only key read there), else the folder's non-hidden child repos with an `origin` remote or `tracker.web`. Child repos with neither are listed under `Not read:`.
- **Waiting on you** comes first and covers every repo, each item as `owner/repo#N`. Each repo's own sections follow. A repo with nothing merged, ruled or moved and no failed read or run is one line (`acme/exemplar: nothing since 2026-10-10 09:00; main push: passed`). A shared `setup:` line is said once, with the repos it applies to (`all 7 repos` when it fits all of them).
- Each repo keeps its own config, window and marker. A repo whose read failed keeps its marker, while the others move theirs. The header names the held repo and the command exits 1. A repo that can't be opened at all is one `FAILED` line. `--json` prints every repo's report.
- `next`, `groom` and the others name the repos they found and ask for `--repo <dir>`. `commands/catchup.md` handles the workspace report instead of stopping, and `commands/next.md` has Claude pick a repo.

**Yours to merge.** #75's run showed "Waiting on you: nothing" while two green PRs the owner had opened waited for the owner to merge them. Catchup now lists an open PR you opened as `yours to merge` when it isn't a draft, has no review requested and no changes requested, has no known conflict (`unknown` is listed and shown as unknown), and has passing checks or none. The recorded lokkju/skills fixture now shows its #38 that way. I left out the age threshold the issue floated; the standing count already covers PRs that haven't moved in the window.

A read-only live run against `~/projects/codexpublicus` (`--no-mark`) read all seven repos in one report and exited 0. Four of them collapsed to one line each, and one setup line covered all seven.

Left for later: `org:` at the workspace root, which would read an org's repos from the forge. Catchup reads local clones, and a repo with no clone has no config file or changelog to read.

Tests: detection with the git keys (precedence, path splitting, bad values), the CLI end to end with an SSH-alias origin, and a workspace of real temp git repos against fake forges and the recorded lokkju/skills fixture.

Closes #71
Closes #75

response.body:
**Problem.** `/forge-tracker:catchup` assumes the session starts in one repo. A session started in a workspace folder that holds several repos (here `~/projects/codexpublicus/`, with citare, citation-bench, codexpublicus.org, exemplar, gorsuch-library, infra and stare, but no `.git` of its own) gets exit 2:

```
forge-tracker: /home/lokkju/projects/codexpublicus has no origin remote (or isn't a git repo)
```

The skill text then says to stop. The workaround was a loop: `git -C <repo> fetch` and `forge-tracker --repo <repo> catchup` for each of the seven, then hand-merging seven reports. Each report also repeats the same config notes (`labels.needs_human`, `labels.decision` and `ruling_pattern` unset), so the useful lines get buried.

**Fix.**
- **Discover the repos.** When the start directory isn't a git repo, treat its immediate children that have an `origin` remote as the workspace. Also accept an explicit list or a forge org in config (e.g. `repos:` or `org: codexpublicus` in `.claude/forge-tracker.local.md` at the workspace root), and a `--workspace DIR` flag.
- **Report them together.** One report, with a combined **Waiting on you** first, each item tagged with its repo, then per-repo **Merged since**, **Decisions made**, **Board movement** and **Health**. Repos where nothing happened collapse to one line ("exemplar: nothing; main push: none"). Config notes appear once, listing the repos they apply to.
- **Keep markers per repo.** If one repo's read fails, only that repo's marker stays, and the exit status says which.
- **Update the skill text.** The catchup skill should run the workspace form instead of stopping when the start directory is a workspace. The same applies to `/forge-tracker:next`.

**A related gap the run showed.** "Waiting on you" was `nothing` in all seven repos, while two PRs sat waiting for the owner to merge them: [codexpublicus/stare#152](https://github.com/codexpublicus/stare/pull/152) and [codexpublicus/citare#71](https://github.com/codexpublicus/citare/pull/71). Both are green, opened by the owner's own account, with no review requested. On a solo repo that's the normal shape of "waiting on me". Consider listing green, mergeable, non-draft PRs older than some threshold, or PRs opened from the owner's account, as waiting on the owner when the repo has no other reviewers.

response.body:
Part of #12 (forge-tracker). Builds on the forge read layer (#21). Like `/catchup`, it can ship for one forge first.

**`/next`** recommends what to work on: the user's own queue, work agents can start now, and what is blocked. It is read-only. It recommends, and never claims, assigns, comments or branches.

**Two layers, both cached outside the repo** under `${XDG_CACHE_HOME:-~/.cache}/<plugin>/next/<host>_<project>/`:
1. **Facts (a script).**
   - **What it reads:** open issues with tier, due date, labels, owners and links; open PRs/MRs with head pipeline and conflict state; branches with no PR/MR.
   - **How it caches:** under a fingerprint of cheap inputs. These are the default-branch head, the newest issue, PR and pipeline `updated_at`, open issue and PR counts, a digest of the milestones (id, title, due date), the remote branch heads, and a schema tag that hashes the code itself. When the fingerprint is unchanged, the cached facts are reused, so a rerun takes seconds. A run with a failed read is written but never reused.
2. **The slate (Claude's ranking).** It is stored with the facts' fingerprint and shown again unchanged until the fingerprint moves.
   - **The user's queue:** person-only items, ordered by how many agent-ready items each one unblocks, counted transitively through blocking links and cycle-safe.
   - **Agent lanes:** unblocked agent-ready items by tier and due date, grouped into lanes that shouldn't touch the same files. The grouping is a stated judgement, not a measurement. A lane that already has an open PR or a pushed branch is marked in flight.
   - **Blocked:** each blocked item and what it waits on.

**Classification rules learned the hard way:**
- **What person-only means:** the configured decision or needs-human labels, plus configurable keyword markers (e.g. hardware, legal).
- **Not person-only:** an assignee is never a reason, because agents share the user's account. Show the assignee as an owner. Some markers are only hints Claude may overrule; design work an agent can build is one example.
- **Merged-but-open issues inflate the ready list badly.** Flag issues that a merged PR/MR references but that are still open. That check, and fixing it, belongs to `/groom` (#22).

**Future enhancement, not now:** a status pane that shows the slate's top items, its age and a "stale" flag when the fingerprint moves. It reads only the cache, and shares a display mechanism with the session-decisions pane.
response.title: forge-tracker: /next, your queue, agent lanes that can start now, and what is blocked

Claude Code 2.1.300 fails `claude plugin validate --strict .` on this marketplace: `plugins[4].name "claude-session-index"` is reserved, since third-party plugin names can't start with `claude-`, `anthropic-`, `anthropics-` or `cc-plugin-`.

- `.claude-plugin/marketplace.json`: the entry is now `session-history`, still sourced from github lokkju/claude-session-index.
- README: the plugin list names `session-history` and gives the migration steps. AGENTS.md notes the reserved prefixes.
- CI pins Claude Code 2.1.300 (was 2.1.286), so strict validation catches this again.

With 2.1.300 locally, `validate --strict` passes on the marketplace and on all four `plugins/*`; the only other output is advice about README install lines for forge-release, forge-tracker and term-recorder, which doesn't change the verdict and isn't touched here. `claude plugin test plugins/session-decisions`: 93 pass, 0 fail.

The plugin side of the rename (its `plugin.json` name and a `hooks.json` that 2.1.300 also rejected) is [lokkju/claude-session-index#2](https://github.com/lokkju/claude-session-index/pull/2). Merge that first, or a fresh install of `session-history@lokkju` gets a plugin whose manifest still says `claude-session-index`.

## Migration

If you installed the plugin under its old name:

```bash
claude plugin uninstall claude-session-index@lokkju
claude plugin marketplace update lokkju
claude plugin install session-history@lokkju
```

The `claude-session-index` CLI installed with `uv tool install` needs nothing.

response.body:
Part of #22. Phase 4 of [the forge-tracker spec](docs/specs/forge-tracker.md): `/groom` on GitHub, the unclear bucket, and the write operations it applies.

## What it does

`forge-tracker groom` is read-only. It runs the spec's checks and sorts what they find into proposals (each a named write with its payload and evidence), an unclear bucket that is never acted on, and a list for the user:

| Check | Proposes | Unclear instead |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Merged but still open | `close` with a comment naming the PR, when a merged PR has a real closing reference (`closedByPullRequestsReferences`) and its merge commit is on the default branch (`compare <default>...<sha>` is `behind` or `identical`) | a `#N` only in a merged PR's title or branch (D22); a closing reference from a PR merged into another branch, or whose merge commit isn't on the default branch |
| Tier label vs milestone | `labels` (add the missing tier label) or `milestone` (when exactly one open milestone fits) | label and milestone disagree; no single fitting milestone |
| Blocked label with nothing linked | `unlink` the label | |
| Link to a closed blocker | `unlink` the link, with the blocker's close date | |
| Decided but still waiting | `labels`: remove needs-human/decision, add `decision_made` (D20), when a `ruling_pattern` comment is newer than the label's newest `labeled` event | no label event to compare against |
| Stale branch | `delete-branch` when there's no open PR and `ahead_by == 0` | commits not on the default branch, when idle past `stale_days` or the branch of a merged PR |
| Conflicted or stale PRs | listed for you | `conflicts: unknown` |
| Likely duplicates | | every pair (token-set similarity of titles and labels, open issues plus those closed in 30 days) |
| Placeholder due dates | listed for you | |

Every check fails on its own: a failed read puts `<check>: FAILED (<reason>)` under a FAILED heading, the command exits 1, and nothing from that check reads as clean. A check whose config is unset is listed as skipped with the key it needs. `--json` carries each proposal's id, op and payload.

## The write layer and approval

There was no write layer yet, so this builds the part of it `/groom` needs, as the spec's Writes section describes:

- `writes.py` holds the only write transport (POST, PATCH and DELETE under the repo's own REST path, nothing else, never GraphQL) and the five operations `/groom` proposes: `close`, `labels`, `milestone`, `unlink`, `delete-branch`. Payloads are validated before anything is sent. The operations that can go stale check first through the read transport: `close` refuses an issue already closed, `unlink` a blocker that reopened, `delete-branch` a branch that moved off the checked sha or is protected.
- With `write_wrapper:` set, forge-tracker sends no write of its own: it runs `<wrapper> <op>` in the repo root with the JSON on stdin, and a non-zero exit refuses, with its stderr shown (D18).
- Every operation, written, refused or failed, is appended to `${XDG_CACHE_HOME}/forge-tracker/writes/<host>_<project>.jsonl` (0600).
- `forge-tracker groom apply` reads `{"approved": [ids]}` on stdin, re-runs every check, and refuses the whole list (exit 2, nothing written) when any id isn't a current proposal. Then it writes the approved ones one at a time and prints a result line for each.
- `forge-tracker write <op>` runs one operation, as the spec names it.
- `commands/groom.md` presents the proposals grouped by kind, asks once (numbers, `all`, `none`), and only then pipes exactly the approved ids to `groom apply`. It forbids writing any other way, and an agent running `/groom` for itself never applies.

The adapter gained `milestones`, `label_events`, `issue_comments` and `on_branch`; `closing_refs` now carries the PR title and merge sha, blocking links the blocker's close date, and branches their protection and head-commit date.

## Tests

310 pass. A fake forge has one case per check and the golden report; each read is broken in turn to show its check FAILED alone; apply runs against a fake write transport (exact methods, paths and bodies), with and without a fake wrapper, and refuses stale, unclear and malformed approvals with nothing sent. `groom-lokkju-skills.json` is a read-only `--record` run against this repo, scrubbed and thinned like the other fixtures. No test, and nothing during development, wrote to a forge.

## Open questions

The spec doesn't settle these; I picked what fits it best:

1. **Merged-PR lookback.** 90 days, for the named-only check and the "branch of merged #N" note. Closing references cover every open issue regardless of age.
2. **Tier pairing.** `tiers.labels[n]` pairs with `tiers.milestone_prefixes[n]`, by position; the check needs both.
3. **Placeholder due dates.** On GitHub a due date belongs to a milestone, so every issue in one shares it by design. I flag a date only when more than one open milestone uses it.
4. **Unmerged branches.** The spec puts a branch whose commits aren't all on the default branch in the unclear bucket. Listing every work-in-progress branch would bury the report, so it's unclear only when idle past `stale_days` (default 14) or when it's a merged PR's branch. Protected branches, the default branch and release and dependency bot branches (`yeet/*`, `release-please--*`, `changeset-release/*`, `dependabot/*`, `renovate/*`) are never looked at; `groom.keep_branches` (globs) adds to that list.
5. **Squash merges.** By the spec's `ahead_by == 0` rule, a squash-merged branch is never a delete proposal, only unclear. This repo merges with merge commits, so its merged branches do show up as proposals.
6. **`forge-tracker write`** is exposed now, as the spec names it, ahead of phase 2's working rules. `/groom` never calls it directly.
7. **Umbrella issues** whose sub-issues are all closed aren't in the spec's check table, so there's no such check.
8. The `unlink` of a native link uses `DELETE /repos/{o}/{r}/issues/{n}/dependencies/blocked_by/{issue_id}`, tested only against the fake transport.

session-decisions picks a repo's forge from its `origin` remote. It uses the built-in host rules and then the `forge_hosts` plugin option from [#57](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/pull/57). Both are global: one host maps to one forge kind for every repo. Some repos need their own answer:

- The remote is an SSH host alias (`github.com-work`, `homelab-git`). The link then uses the alias as its web host, and that host doesn't resolve.
- The remote is a mirror or a push-only URL, and issues live on a different forge. For example, the code is on GitHub but the tracker is a Forgejo instance.
- The SSH host and the web host differ, such as `ssh.git.lab.example.com` against `git.lab.example.com`, or the web UI sits under a subpath.

The fix is a per-repo override that wins over `forge_hosts` and the built-in rules. It would set the forge kind and the web base URL, for example `forgejo` and `https://git.lab.lokkju.com/lokkju/demo`, with an optional host override. Where it could live:

- `git config` in the repo: `git config session-decisions.forge forgejo`, `git config session-decisions.web https://...`. It's per clone, needs no new file, and is read by the same `git` call that already reads the remote.
- The repo's `.claude/settings.json` or `settings.local.json`, under `pluginConfigs`, if Claude Code honours plugin options at project scope.
- A small file in `.claude/`, if forge-tracker ends up with per-repo forge config too, so the two can share it.

forge-tracker resolves the same question for its own reports, so whichever mechanism is chosen should be one both plugins read.

Related: [#54](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/54), [#57](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/pull/57).
response.title: session-decisions: per-repo forge override (kind and web base), ahead of forge_hosts

response.body:
A clone can now say which forge its `#12` and `!4` references link to, ahead of `forge_hosts` and the built-in host rules:

```bash
git config tracker.forge forgejo
git config tracker.web https://git.lab.lokkju.com/lokkju/demo
```

## Why git config

I weighed the three places [#60](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/60) names:

- **git config** is per clone, which is where an SSH host alias belongs (it comes from one machine's `~/.ssh/config`, so a committed file would be wrong for other clones). git parses it, the plugin reads it with one more `git` call next to the remote lookup, and forge-tracker's Python can read it with `git config --get` and no parser. `includeIf "hasconfig:remote.*.url:..."` in `~/.gitconfig` can apply `tracker.forge` to every clone of an alias.
- **Project-scoped plugin options** are per plugin, so forge-tracker couldn't read session-decisions' value without reaching into another plugin's settings, and `.claude/settings.json` is committed.
- **A `.claude/` file**: forge-tracker already has `.claude/forge-tracker.local.md` with a `forge:` key, but its loader rejects unknown keys (there's no `web:`), session-decisions would need a frontmatter parser, and a committed file has the same alias problem.

The keys are `tracker.*`, not `session-decisions.*`, so both plugins can read them. Magit Forge already uses the `forge.*` section, so I avoided that one.

## Behaviour

- `tracker.web` set: it is the repository (`https://` only), and the remote isn't read. The kind is `tracker.forge`, or else whatever `forge_hosts` and the built-in rules say of the web host.
- Only `tracker.forge` set: the remote's host and path on that kind of forge.
- Neither set: the existing behaviour, unchanged.
- A subpath works for GitHub and Forgejo (`https://code.example.org/forge/me/tool`, cross-repo refs included). For GitLab the whole path is the project, so `group/project#7` misses a subpath; the README says so.
- A value it can't use gets a toast at session start, the same way `forge_hosts` does, and is ignored.

The pure logic (`parseOverride`, `webForge`, `resolveForge`) lives in `hooks/forge.ts` with tests; `register.tsx` reads `git config --get-regexp '^tracker\.(forge|web)$'` at session start.

## Verified

- `claude plugin test plugins/session-decisions`: 93 pass. `claude plugin validate --strict plugins/session-decisions` passes.
- On screen with term-recorder: Claude Code 2.1.300, Sonnet, `--plugin-dir` on this branch, in a scratch repo whose `origin` is `homelab-git:lokkju/demo.git` with both keys set. One `DECIDE ... [#12]` task drew the D1 card, and the cast has the OSC 8 hyperlink `https://git.lab.lokkju.com/lokkju/demo/issues/12` on its `#12`.
- The `includeIf hasconfig` glob in the README (`homelab-git:*/**`) was checked against git 2.43; `homelab-git:**` doesn't match a path with a slash.

forge-tracker doesn't read the keys yet; that's a follow-up there.

Closes #60
response.title: feat(session-decisions): per-repo forge override in git config (tracker.forge, tracker.web)

response.body:
Part of #12 (forge-tracker). Builds on the forge read layer (#21). Each command can ship for one forge first, but the layer is what makes it work on GitHub, GitLab and Forgejo alike.

**`/catchup`** is for coming back to a project after time away: what changed, and what is waiting on you. It is read-only: no claims, comments or merges.

**The window:**
- It starts where the user's previous successful `/catchup` ended, kept in a local marker. **Not** at "your last forge activity": agents act under the user's account, and in practice that gives a four-minute window opening at an agent's last push.
- The marker lives under `${XDG_CACHE_HOME:-~/.cache}/<plugin>/catchup/<host>_<project>_<user>.json`. The directory is 0700 and files 0600, writes are atomic, and a relative XDG value is ignored.
- The next window starts a few minutes before the marker, so a fast local clock can't skip events. Seeing an event twice is harmless.
- The marker moves only when every read succeeded, and only after the report has printed. A failed print restores the old marker.
- With no marker, the first run covers 7 days. `--since` is an ad-hoc look back that neither reads nor moves the marker. `--no-mark` gives a dry look, and agents must use it whenever they run the command for their own purposes.

**Sections, in order:**
1. **Waiting on you.**
   - Mentions of you in the window, and open PRs/MRs where you are reviewer or assignee.
   - Issues assigned to you and issues carrying the configured needs-a-human and decision labels. Only items created or updated in the window are listed in full; the standing backlog is one count line per list.
   - An issue on several lists is listed once and counted in each. `--all` lists everything.
2. **Merged since:** PRs/MRs merged in the window, grouped by the issue numbers in their titles or branches (ignore date-shaped branch segments). It also covers changelog entries added, where the repo has a configured changelog or records file.
3. **Decisions made:** comments in the window matching a configured ruling pattern, e.g. `Ruling (YYYY-MM-DD):`.
4. **Board movement:** issues opened and closed, counted by the configured priority tiers (labels first, milestone as fallback).
5. **Health:** the default branch's newest push pipeline/run and its failed jobs, a failed scheduled run on its own line, flaky jobs (passed only on retry more than once), and the configured release/registry tags.

**Output:** text by default, `--json` for the same data. Exit 0 only when every read succeeded. The slash command tells Claude to summarize with Waiting on you first, to state every FAILED part plainly, and to act on nothing unless asked.

**Config** (in forge-tracker's per-repo file): tier labels or milestone prefixes, the needs-human, decision and blocked label names, the ruling pattern, the changelog path, and the tags to report.
response.title: forge-tracker: /catchup, what changed and what waits on you since your last catchup

A session-decisions test run on Claude Code 2.1.300 (`--model haiku`, `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TODO_TOOLS=1`) queued its hand-offs with `decision_add` instead of TaskCreate. I took that for missing task tools at first; they weren't missing.

**What changed in 2.1.300.** The `haiku` alias now resolves to `claude-haiku-5-5` (2.1.286 had `haiku:{default:"claude-haiku-4-5"}`; 2.1.300 has `haiku:{default:"claude-haiku-5-5",per_provider:{bedrock:"claude-haiku-4-5",vertex:"claude-haiku-4-5",...}}`). The gate itself is unchanged; it's the same function under new minified names:

```js
function TV(){if(hc()||YUo())return!0;let e=$Lt();if(e===void 0||p6r(e)||f6r(e))return!0;return a.CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TODO_TOOLS===!0}
function roe(){return NP()&&TV()}   // NP(): false only when CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TASKS is false
```

The model allow-list (`c6r`) still stops at `claude-haiku-4-5`, so haiku now needs the env var like every other Claude 5 model. TaskCreate, TaskUpdate, TaskList and TaskGet are `shouldDefer:!0` in both 2.1.286 and 2.1.300, so with the env var they arrive in the deferred-tool list, not the initial one.

**What I checked** (one short turn each, 100x30 via term-record, plus two `-p` runs):

| Model (`--model`) | Mode | `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TODO_TOOLS` | Task tools |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| haiku (Haiku 5.5) | interactive | unset | absent |
| haiku (Haiku 5.5) | interactive | 1 | all four, deferred |
| sonnet (Sonnet 5.5) | interactive | unset | absent |
| sonnet (Sonnet 5.5) | interactive | 1 | all four, deferred |
| haiku (Haiku 5.5) | `-p` | unset | absent (init lists only `Task`, `TaskStop`) |
| haiku (Haiku 5.5) | `-p` | 1 | all four, deferred |

The failing run's transcript has `deferred_tools_delta` naming TaskCreate, TaskGet, TaskList and TaskUpdate, so the session had them. The model called `ToolSearch` with `select:mcp__session-decisions__decision_add` straight after the hand-off nudge, which said "goes in the decision queue with TaskCreate (or decision_add)".

**Changes.**

- `hooks/handoff.ts`: the nudge says TaskCreate is a deferred tool to load with ToolSearch, and that decision_add is only for a session without TaskCreate. With this change, the same two-turn scenario on Haiku 5.5 called `ToolSearch select:TaskCreate` and then TaskCreate for A1 and A2 (one run, so this is evidence, not proof).
- session-decisions README: notes that `haiku` is Haiku 5.5 on the Anthropic API since 2.1.300.
- term-recorder SKILL.md: the task-tool note covers `-p` too, says haiku is a Claude 5 model now, and says the tools are deferred.

`record-demo.sh` already sets `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TODO_TOOLS=1` and defaults to sonnet, so it needed no change.

response.body:
When a repo has no `.claude/forge-tracker.local.md`, the plugin degrades quietly and never offers to fix it. It just emits parenthetical notes, every run, forever.

First use on `eltorocorp/terraform-et-github` at `2026.10.15.3`, with no config file present:

```
/catchup
  (labels.needs_human isn't set, so needs-human issues aren't listed)
  (labels.decision isn't set, so decision issues aren't listed)
  (ruling_pattern isn't set, so rulings aren't picked out)

/next
  Your queue
    nothing person-only
  (labels.needs_human isn't set, so no label marks needs-human items)
  (labels.decision isn't set, so no label marks decision items)
```

The notes are honest, and I would not want them removed. The problem is that nothing ever converts them into configuration.

## Why it matters more than a missing nicety

`Your queue: nothing person-only` is the headline of `/next`, and with no labels configured it is **structurally incapable of being anything else**. The queue is populated from `labels.needs_human`, `labels.decision` and person-only markers; with none set, the only path left is a marker word in a body. So the report's most prominent line reads as "nothing needs you" when what it means is "no label was configured to say so."

Someone reading it quickly — which is the whole point of a catchup — takes the wrong conclusion. The degradation is silent in effect even though it is documented in a footnote.

## Ask

On the first activation or first use in a session, when no `.claude/forge-tracker.local.md` exists for the repo, ask whether the user wants to configure it, and offer to write it.

The machinery is mostly there already. `config.py` knows the full key set — `LABEL_KEYS = ("needs_human", "decision", "decision_made", "blocked", "agent")` plus `ruling_pattern` and friends — and the commands already detect and report which are unset. What is missing is the prompt and the writer.

A good version would be concrete rather than open-ended, since the useful answer depends on labels that already exist on the forge: read the repo's actual label list, propose plausible mappings from it (`needs-human`, `needs-decision`, `blocked`, `agent` or whatever is really there), and let the user confirm, correct or skip. Offering a free-text config file to fill in by hand is the version people decline.

## Constraints worth keeping

Ask **once** per repo and remember a decline, so the prompt does not reappear every session; a nag is worse than the footnotes. `/catchup` and `/next` are documented read-only, so the prompt belongs at activation or behind an explicit confirmation, and writing the file should be the only side effect. A repo that genuinely has no such labels should be able to record that fact, so the footnotes stop rather than persisting as noise.
response.title: forge-tracker: offer to configure labels on first use; an unconfigured repo silently reports an empty queue

response.body:
On a repo with no `.claude/forge-tracker.local.md`, the reports printed two or three parenthetical notes every run and nothing turned them into configuration. `/next`'s `Your queue: nothing person-only` read as "nothing needs you" when it meant no label was configured to say so.

What changes:

- **One `setup:` line.** Both reports replace their per-key notes with a single line that names what's missing, what the report can't do without it, and how to set it up (`forge-tracker labels suggest`). `/next` appends `(but labels aren't configured to mark any; see setup)` to an empty queue. The Decisions made section of `/catchup` points at the setup line.
- **`~` records "none".** A label key or `ruling_pattern` set to `~` (or `null`) records that the repo has no such label or convention, and the reports drop the line. A quoted `'null'` is still a label name.
- **`forge-tracker labels suggest`** reads the repo's labels (`GET /repos/{o}/{r}/labels`, through the read transport) and prints a proposed file: roles matched by name patterns (`needs-human`, `human`, `needs-decision`, `decision`, `question`, `decided`, `blocked`, `on-hold`, `agent-ready`, `agent`, ...), the largest priority family as tiers (`P0`.., `priority:N`, `priority: high`), `~` for each unmatched role, and a `gh label create` command for each. An existing file keeps its values, and the proposal lists only the keys it lacks. It writes nothing; `--json` prints the same data.
- **`forge-tracker labels decline`** records a no in `${XDG_CACHE_HOME}/forge-tracker/setup/<host>_<project>.json` (0600, no forge read, no token). The setup line then says `Setup was declined on <date>`.
- **`/catchup` and `/next`** offer setup once when the line is present and not declined (and not for an agent's own run). They show the proposal, write `.claude/forge-tracker.local.md` only on the user's yes, and on a no run `labels decline`. There's no write layer yet, so missing labels on the forge stay `gh label create` commands for the user to run. The reports themselves remain read-only.

The two report modules change only where they built the old notes: two short swaps in `catchup.py`, plus the note swap and the empty-queue suffix in `next.py`. `forges/github.py` gains a `labels()` read and `model.py` a `Label`. The recorded `/next` golden changes in its queue and note lines only.

Tests: matching, tier families, quoting round-trips through the parser, the proposed file loading and silencing the setup line, merge with an existing file, the CLI over a fake label list (GET only, nothing written), a failed read, and decline (0600 file, no `gh` call). README and spec updated.

Closes #59
response.title: feat(forge-tracker): offer label setup on first use

response.body:
The skill says that every question or step only the user can do goes in the queue in the same turn. Nothing enforces it. An assistant can end a reply with a "left for you" list (merge these PRs, run this on each host) and queue none of it. Wording alone relies on the model applying the rule at the moment it writes the closing list, and that is where it slips. The usual rationalization is that a step the assistant could do on request (merging a PR) isn't "only the user's".

## Proposal

- **A `classic.Stop` handler in `hooks/register.tsx`.** It reads `last_assistant_message` and skips when `stop_hook_active` is set. It finds hand-off lines that carry no `D<n>`/`A<n>` label: phrases such as "left for you", "you'll need to", "your call" and "next steps", plus the bullets or numbered items that follow them. When it finds any, it returns `block` with a reason that quotes those lines and says to queue them and rewrite the reply. The reason also says to ignore a match that isn't a hand-off.
- **The detector in `hooks/queue.ts` or `hooks/subject.ts`,** as plain data, with tests for:
  - hand-offs with labels
  - hand-offs without labels
  - prose that only resembles one
- **One line in SKILL.md:** anything handed back to the user counts, including merges and per-host steps the assistant could do if asked.
- **Release:** a minor version, 2.1.0.

## Costs and open questions

- It adds one model pass to each reply where it fires.
- Phrase matching misfires both ways. The phrase list and the threshold need tuning against real transcripts before it blocks by default. One option is to start it as an `additionalContext` nudge rather than a block.
- It's unclear whether the fallback-ledger mode (no TaskCreate) needs the same check, since its replies already end with a list of open items.

Found while settling the last question on [lokkju/skills#13](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/13), on Claude Code 2.1.286 in headless `claude -p` runs with `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_FUNCTION_HOOKS=1` and `CLAUDE_CODE_ENABLE_TODO_TOOLS=1`, session-decisions 2026.10.15.1 installed.

**What happens.** The parent creates D1 with TaskCreate. A background subagent (`Agent` with `run_in_background: true`) is told the user answered D1 and to settle it. The subagent has no TaskUpdate: it isn't in its tool list and `ToolSearch` `select:TaskUpdate` answers "No matching deferred tools found". So it calls `decision_close`, which refuses:

> session-decisions: D1 is a task-list item; mark it completed with TaskUpdate and add the ruling to its description. If TaskUpdate is deferred, load it with ToolSearch first.

The ruling is recorded nowhere and the task file stays pending. `decision_update` goes through the same `TaskUpdate` check, so I'd expect it to dead-end the same way (not run).

**Why.** `taskUpdateOffered()` in `hooks/register.tsx` asks `$.tool.list()`. A probe hook logged that list inside the subagent's `decision_close` call (the `tool.call` event carried the subagent's `agentId`), and it named TaskCreate, TaskGet, TaskList, TaskStop and TaskUpdate: the main loop's tools, not the subagent's. The declaration says "the tools the model can call now", which isn't what it returned for a subagent's loop.

**Related, documentation only.** A background subagent gets no TaskCreate either, so its items go through `decision_add` and are ledger items: they share the parent's queue and counter (the subagent's item came back as D2 after the parent's D1) but never appear in ctrl+t, even though the parent's do. The README's "Without them" paragraph and the ctrl+t limit describe a session with no task tools; they don't cover a session whose background subagents lack them. A foreground subagent does get TaskCreate, and its items land in the parent's task list with the parent's labels.

The fix is the maintainer's call; options I can see are deciding from the loop (`e.agentId` is set on a subagent's `tool.call`, and `$.agent.list()` lists the loop by that id, though it has no background flag), or letting `decision_close` settle a task-list item when the call comes from a subagent.
response.title: session-decisions: decision_close dead-ends in a background subagent ($.tool.list() reports the parent's TaskUpdate)

An ACTION item whose subject has a top-level `(recommend ...)` clause now gets an **Accept** button beside **Done**. It answers `A<k>: go with <recommendation>`, the same wording as a DECIDE item's Accept, and those items join **Accept all**. The recommendation comes from the existing `splitBody`/`recommendation()` in `hooks/subject.ts`, so it's the item's own last top-level `(recommend ...)`, as #132 settled.

- **Details view** (from `[more]`, the card's label, or the transcript's `queued A1` line): the same Accept/Done pair.
- **Chip**: `recommends <choice>` already drew for any kind, so ACTION items with a recommendation show it with no change.

- **Skill**: an ACTION item that waits only on the user's approval for a step the agent carries out (merge, apply, tag, deploy) carries a `(recommend ...)` clause. `A2: go with <choice>` means do the step, then close the item with the result; `A2: done` means the user did it. The README describes both buttons.
- **Tests** (`tests/register.test.tsx`): an ACTION item with and without a recommendation (buttons, Done's variant, the answer text), Accept all mixing a DECIDE with two ACTION items (one without a recommendation, which it skips), Accept all showing for two recommended actions alone, and the details view's buttons and Accept answer.

response.body:
`/groom` finds merged-but-open issues only when a merge commit or PR body carries a closing
reference (`Closes #N`). In a repo where work lands without them, that whole class is invisible,
and those issues accumulate silently — which is the failure mode `/groom` exists to catch.

## What happened

On a private repo with 47 open issues, `/groom` proposed 6 fixes: 2 `link-add`, 4
`delete-branch`. It proposed **zero** closes.

Five of those open issues were in fact complete, delivered across two large merged PRs. Neither
merge commit used a closing keyword, so `/groom` could not see any of them. A human spotted all
five by reading the issue titles against what had shipped, and closed them by hand.

## Why this is worth fixing rather than just writing better commit messages

The closing-reference convention fails in exactly the repos that need grooming most: ones where
work lands in large PRs, where one issue is satisfied by several commits across several PRs, or
where the PR predates the issue. `/groom` already reads merged PRs since a date — it has the
titles and the changed paths in hand.

It is also the one proposal class where being wrong is cheap: a wrongly-closed issue is
reopened in one click, unlike a deleted branch or a written link.

## Possible shapes, least invasive first

1. **A "possibly done" section, listed rather than proposed** — same status as the existing
   *Listed for you* items. Name the issue, the merged PR that looks like it, and the signal
   (title overlap, or the issue naming a path that PR changed). No write, no approval, no risk.
   This alone would have surfaced all five.
2. **A proposal class gated on stronger evidence** — the issue's body names a path or symbol a
   merged PR changed, *and* the issue has had no activity since that merge. Proposed by number
   like any other fix.
3. **Ask the forge.** GitHub's timeline API records `cross-referenced` events when a PR mentions
   an issue in any form, not only with closing keywords. Cheaper than diffing, and already on
   the wire.

## What I would not do

Don't infer closure from label or milestone state, and don't close on title similarity alone.
Both would produce confident wrong closes in a repo with near-duplicate issues, which is the
other thing `/groom` is meant to find.

## A smaller, related observation from the same run

The report's *Skipped (not configured)* section correctly named three checks that need
`.claude/forge-tracker.local.md`. That part works and the message is clear.

But the combination — no label config *and* no closing references — meant `/groom` had almost
nothing to work with, and nothing in the output said so. The report reads the same whether it
ran every check and found little, or ran two checks out of six. A line stating which checks
actually ran, rather than only which were skipped, would set expectations honestly and would
have prompted a closer look sooner.
response.title: forge-tracker /groom cannot see merged-but-open issues without a closing reference

response.body:
In the session-decisions panel, a DECIDE item with a recommendation gets an **Accept** button, which answers `D<k>: go with <recommendation>`, and it counts toward **Accept all**. An ACTION item gets only **Done**, even when its subject carries a recommendation.

In practice many ACTION items are approvals the agent can carry out once the user says go, and they come with a recommendation:

```
A12 ACTION: approve merging owner/repo#34 (CI green) (recommend merge) [owner/repo#34]
A13 ACTION: approve merging owner/repo#56 and tagging v1.2.0 (recommend merge and tag) [owner/repo#56]
```

For these, **Done** is the wrong word: the user hasn't done anything. They want to approve the step so the agent does it. Today they have to type `A12: go` by hand.

## Proposal

- When an ACTION item's body has a `(recommend ...)` clause, show an **Accept** button beside **Done**. It answers `A<k>: go with <recommendation>`, matching the DECIDE wording, so the agent gets the same signal either way.
- Include those ACTION items in **Accept all** (in `register.tsx`, the `accepts` list now reads the recommendation only for `item.kind === 'DECIDE'`).
- Show the `recommends <choice>` chip on ACTION items that have one, as DECIDE items do.
- Keep **Done** for ACTION items, recommendation or not, for the case where the user really did the step themselves.
- An ACTION item without a recommendation keeps only **Done**.

## Notes

- `recommendation()` and `shortRecommendation()` in `hooks/subject.ts` already parse the clause; the change is which kinds the panel applies them to.
- The skill text (SKILL.md) can say ACTION items that need the user's approval should carry a `(recommend ...)` clause, so they get the button.
- Tests: `tests/register.test.tsx` covering an ACTION item with and without a recommendation, and Accept all mixing both kinds.
response.title: session-decisions: an Accept button for ACTION items that carry a recommendation

The plugins here are written for Claude Code. #118 (merged as #123) made the skills' scripts portable: each script now lives in its skill's own directory and SKILL.md calls it through `${CLAUDE_SKILL_DIR}`, so a skill installed by `npx skills add`, OpenCode's `skills` config or a plain skills folder can run it. That fixes the paths, nothing more. This issue is the rest: port what can be ported to other harnesses, starting with OpenCode, and give the plugins that need it a per-harness layer.

**What each plugin depends on today:**
- **forge-release, forge-tracker, worktree-tidy, term-recorder:** a skill plus standard-library Python. These should mostly work anywhere once the paths are right. Claude Code-only pieces:
  - the slash commands (`commands/*.md`);
  - worktree-tidy's session-start hook (`hooks/hooks.json`);
  - term-recorder's `allowed-tools` pre-approval;
  - forge-tracker's catchup/next/groom commands.
- **session-decisions:** a Claude Code function-hooks mod (pane, TaskCreate labelling, hand-off checks, `decision_*` tools) plus a skill. Only the skill and its no-plugin fallback (#114) work elsewhere.
- **session-history:** wraps the claude-session-index CLI, which reads Claude Code transcripts.

**To decide and build:**
1. **Survey:** for each plugin, list what works unchanged in OpenCode, what needs a per-harness equivalent (commands, hooks, tool pre-approval, MCP tools, a UI surface) and what can't port. Test with a real OpenCode install, not from docs alone.
2. **Layout for per-harness parts:** for example `plugins/<name>/harness/<harness>/` next to the shared skill and scripts, with the shared skill text written harness-neutral and each harness's extras (OpenCode plugin/commands, Claude Code hooks/commands) kept beside it. Record the convention in AGENTS.md, as was done for the minimum Claude Code version.
3. **OpenCode first:** port the skill-plus-script plugins and their commands. For session-decisions, decide whether an OpenCode plugin (its plugin API, a TUI or tool surface) can carry the queue, or whether the skill's labelled-list fallback is the OpenCode story.
4. **CI:** at least a smoke test that each portable skill's script runs from a skills-folder install, not only from the Claude Code plugin cache.
5. **Install docs** per harness in each README and the top-level README.

Related: #118 and #123 (paths), #114 (session-decisions' no-plugin fallback), #124 (minimum Claude Code version), lokkju/infra#214 (headless agents for the cattle runner, which may pick OpenCode).
response.title: Port the plugins to other harnesses (OpenCode first), with per-harness parts where a plugin needs them

response.body:
Part of #12 (forge-tracker). Builds on the forge read layer (#21), plus a small set of writes.

**`/groom`** keeps the tracker telling the truth, so that `/catchup` and `/next` rank real work. In practice the board drifts in predictable ways, and a ranking built on a drifted board ranks finished work as ready.

**The checks:**
- **Merged but still open:** an issue that a merged PR/MR references (`Closes #N`, `#N` in the title or branch) but that is still open. This is verified against the default branch, not taken on trust.
- **Labels disagreeing with milestones:** a tier label with no matching milestone, or a milestone whose tier label is missing.
- **A blocked label with nothing linked**, or links whose blocker is closed.
- **Decided but still waiting:** an issue labelled needs-a-human or decision that has a ruling comment after the label was added.
- **Stale branches:** remote branches with no open PR/MR whose commits are all on the default branch, so they are candidates to delete.
- **Stale or conflicted PRs/MRs:** open ones with merge conflicts, or no activity for N days.
- **Likely duplicates:** title and term similarity among open issues and those closed recently.
- **Placeholder due dates** shared by many issues, which skew any ordering by due date.

**Behaviour:**
- **Report first, read-only by default.** Every proposed change is listed with its evidence. Nothing is written until the user approves, item by item or as a batch.
- **Approved writes:** close with a resolution comment naming the PR/MR, fix labels or milestones, remove a blocked label, delete a merged branch. Each goes through forge-tracker's optional write-wrapper (#12), so a repo can enforce its own scrubbing or comment format.
- **Never acts on an inference it couldn't verify:** an "unclear" bucket is left for the user.
- **Output:** text and `--json`, with FAILED reads stated plainly, never as an empty section.
response.title: forge-tracker: /groom finds tracker drift (merged-but-open issues, label and milestone mismatches, stale branches) and fixes it on approval

Long Claude Code sessions are hard to navigate: there is no scrollbar or jump-to-position in the terminal UI, and no search over the conversation itself. Research, then build if feasible:

- What exists today: transcript view (ctrl+o), the session JSONL under `~/.claude/projects/`, `/resume`, terminal scrollback and tmux copy-mode search, any statusline or hook APIs that could help.
- Options for search: a skill or slash command that greps the current session's JSONL and prints matching turns with their position; an MCP tool doing the same; a small TUI (fzf over the transcript) launched with `!`.
- Options for a scrollbar or jump: whether the terminal UI exposes anything (likely not); a separate pager view of the transcript (e.g. rendered markdown in `less` or a browser artifact) with anchors per turn.
- File upstream feature requests for whatever needs Claude Code itself.
response.title: Conversation history: search and jump-to in long Claude Code sessions

response.body:
Two session-decisions changes.

**decision_close from a background subagent ([#37](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/37)).** Inside a subagent, `$.tool.list()` answers the main loop's tools (I confirmed it again on 2.1.300: a background subagent's call listed TaskCreate through TaskUpdate), and no hook lists a subagent's own. So a background subagent was told to use a TaskUpdate it doesn't have, and the ruling went nowhere. The plugin now judges the loop that made the call by its `agentId`:

- the main loop: `$.tool.list()`, as before;
- a subagent spawned in the foreground: what the main loop has (recorded from `agent.spawn`'s `background`);
- a subagent that has called a task tool: it has them;
- any other subagent (background, a teammate, a workflow agent, one spawned before the plugin loaded): no TaskUpdate, so `decision_close` settles the task-list item in the queue, the same path a restart that drops the task tools already takes. `decision_update` points it at that path.

The README's "Without them" paragraph now covers background subagents (their items go through `decision_add` into the shared queue and never reach ctrl+t), and the Limits section says how a subagent is judged.

**Hand-off check ([#1](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/1)).** A `classic.Stop` hook reads the final reply for work handed to the user that isn't queued: list items under a hand-off heading (`Left for you:`, `Next steps for you:`, `You'll need to:`) and lines that hand a step over themselves (`you'll need to merge`, `left for you`, `your call`, `please merge #12`, `run these on each host`). When it finds any, it shows a toast (`2 hand-offs not queued: Merge PR #41.`) and hands the model a reminder with the next prompt through `UserPromptSubmit`'s `additionalContext`. It never blocks, and costs no extra model call. I went with a warning and a nudge rather than the issue's `block`, per its own open question about tuning before blocking.

To keep false alarms rare it skips a line that names a label or that an open item (or one queued this turn) covers by reference or by most of its words; conditional, negated and questioning phrasing; code blocks and quotes; a heading that is really a sentence; and a bare `Next steps:`. It stays quiet while a Stop hook continuation is active, and a new `handoff_check` option turns it off. The detector is `hooks/handoff.ts`, with tests for labelled hand-offs, unlabelled ones, and prose that only resembles one. SKILL.md gets the line that merges and per-host steps count.

Verified on screen with term-recorder (Claude Code 2.1.300, haiku): a reply ending in a `Left for you:` list raised the toast, and on the next prompt ("ok") the model queued both items as A1 and A2. A headless `claude -p` run with a background subagent settled the main loop's A1 through `decision_close`.

Closes #37
Closes #1
response.title: feat(session-decisions): flag unqueued hand-offs and settle task items from background subagents

On lokkju/infra (forge-tracker 2026.10.15.1, `catchup`, window 2026-10-08 to 2026-10-15), "Merged since" filed PRs under issues the branch names never meant:

```
#0  1 PR: #279 chore(homelab): GARM runner image 2.338.0
#1  6 PRs: #155 chore(cilium): 1.19.8 ..., #156 chore(cilium): 1.20.2, ...
#2  2 PRs: #156 chore(cilium): 1.20.2, #279 chore(homelab): GARM runner image 2.338.0
#8  2 PRs: ...
#19 2 PRs: ...
#20 1 PR: #156 chore(cilium): 1.20.2
#338 1 PR: #279 chore(homelab): GARM runner image 2.338.0
```

The cause is `issue_numbers()` in `scripts/forge_tracker/catchup.py`. `_DATEISH` only strips runs that start with a four-digit year (`\d{4}[-._]\d{1,2}[-._]\d{1,2}`). A semver run such as `1.20.2` or `2.338.0` in a branch (`garm-runner-2.338.0-38790455020`, `cilium-1.20.2`) survives. The split on `.` then turns it into the segments `2`, `338` and `0`, and each one becomes an issue number. `#0` can never be an issue.

Expected:
- treat any dotted all-digit run (`\d+(?:\.\d+)+`) in a branch as a version, not as issue numbers;
- never emit `0`.

A single all-digit branch segment (`fix-42`) should still count. Add a fixture with the branch shapes above to `tests/test_catchup.py`.
response.title: forge-tracker: /catchup reads version numbers in branch names as issue numbers

response.body:
`/next` ranks issues only. Open PRs never appear, so the thing most likely to be *actually in flight* is invisible in the report that exists to say what to work on.

Observed on `eltorocorp/terraform-et-github` at plugin version `2026.10.15.3`:

```
$ forge-tracker next
Agent-ready ... 15 items, all issues
Blocked         nothing blocked
Flags           8 branches with no PR
```

Meanwhile:

```
$ gh pr list --state open
#260  feat(repos): add mcp-mailgun repository
#259  add helm-forgejo for PoC
#258  Feat/add elboto repo
#254  fix(rulesets): require the dedicated entry point, not et-gh-workflows' own CI
```

None of the four appears anywhere in the report. Confirmed in the facts too, not just the rendering — `forge-tracker next facts --json` gives `in_flight: []` on every one of the 15 items, and `other_branches` lists only branches *without* a PR. There is no PR data in the payload at all.

## This is a spec/implementation gap, not a new feature

#24 already specifies it. From that issue, describing the facts layer:

> **What it reads:** open issues with tier, due date, labels, owners and links; **open PRs/MRs with head pipeline and conflict state**; branches with no PR/MR.

And the `/next` skill text relies on it existing, telling the presenter to keep "each item's in-flight marks (an open PR with its draft, conflict and CI state, or a pushed branch)" and never to call "a lane with `conflicts: unknown` ready to merge". Both instructions are unreachable today, because nothing ever populates `in_flight`.

## Why it bites

The gap is worst in exactly the case the report should be best at. A PR that is open, approved, and stale by a few commits is both the closest thing to done and the easiest to forget; `/next` currently cannot mention it. In the run above, #254 had been open for some weeks, had an approving review, and needed a rebase — none of which surfaced.

It also undercuts lane assignment. A lane cannot be judged safe to start if the report does not know an open PR is already editing those files.

## Shape of the fix

Populate `in_flight` on each item from the PRs that reference it (branch name, `Closes #n`, or a linked issue), and list PRs that reference no issue as their own entries rather than dropping them. The flags section already handles the branch-with-no-PR case; the mirror case, a PR with no issue, has no home today.

Worth carrying through to the report: draft state, mergeable/conflict state (as `unknown` when the forge has not computed it — the skill already says never to present that as clean), review decision, and CI conclusion.
response.title: forge-tracker: /next ignores open PRs entirely; in_flight is never populated

response.body:
Two forge-tracker fixes, one commit each.

**#58, `/next` and open PRs.** The in-flight matching worked: an open PR that closes an issue, says `#N` in its title or has `N` in its branch marks that issue. What failed was everything else. `classify` attached each open PR to the open issues it names and dropped the rest, and the report and `next facts --json` carried no PR data of their own. All four open PRs on eltorocorp/terraform-et-github name no issue (no closing reference, no `#N`, branches like `bprice/mcp-mailgun-repo`), so all four vanished and every item showed `in_flight: []`. The recorded lokkju/skills replay had the same hole: its open release PR #51 appeared nowhere.

- The facts gain `other_changes`: each open PR with no open issue in flight, with draft, conflicts, CI, review decision, author, branch and any issue numbers it names that aren't open.
- The report lists them under "Open PRs with no open issue", after Blocked. When the closing references read fails, the list says a PR on it may still close an open issue.
- The GitHub adapter reads `reviewDecision`; in-flight marks and the new list show it (`review: approved`, `review: changes requested`, `review: review required`).
- The spec, README and `commands/next.md` say where these PRs go. The `next` fixture is re-recorded read-only against lokkju/skills for the new query; it has no open PRs today, so the synthetic tests cover the new section.

**#45, branch numbers.** `catchup.issue_numbers` split branch names on `.`, so `garm-runner-2.338.0-38790455020` filed PR #279 under #2, #338 and #0, and `cilium-1.20.2` under #1, #20 and #2. `next.branch_numbers` was a copy of the same parser. Both now call `refs.branch_numbers`, which keeps a dotted version as one word and counts a number only when it's clearly an issue: a whole word at the start or end of a `/` segment (`21-github-adapter`, `fix/21`, `sd-26`) or after `issue`, `gh`, `fix` and similar words. Dates, run ids and hashes over six digits, leading zeros, middle-of-name numbers (`phase-2-docs`), `0`, and `dependabot/` or `renovate/` branches name nothing. `#0` in a title doesn't count either. `tests/test_refs.py` uses lokkju/infra's real merged branch names.

Closes #58
Closes #45
response.title: fix(forge-tracker): list open PRs with no issue in /next and stop reading versions as issue numbers

Adds a `forge_hosts` option to session-decisions (ruling D30), so issue and pull request references link on a self-hosted forge whose kind the plugin can't tell from the host name. Related: [#54](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/54).

- `plugin.json` declares it as a `userConfig` string field. Claude Code 2.1.286 field types are string, number, boolean, directory and file (string can be `multiple`); there's no object type, so the value is `host=kind` entries split by commas, e.g. `git.lab.lokkju.com=forgejo, code.example.com=gitlab`. Kinds are github, gitlab, forgejo and gitea (gitea links as forgejo).
- `hooks/forge.ts`: `parseForgeHosts` turns the option into a host map plus a note per unusable entry; `forgeOf(remote, hosts)` checks the map before the built-in rules, so an entry wins for its host.
- `hooks/register.tsx` takes the option from `register(on, options)`, toasts the notes once at session start, and passes the map to the remote lookup.
- README documents it under "Forge hosts", with `/config` and `settings.json` (`pluginConfigs["session-decisions@lokkju"].options.forge_hosts`).

Tests cover an unknown host mapped, a built-in host overridden, bad entries skipped with notes while the rest apply, GitLab subgroup paths and Forgejo `/pulls/`, and the wiring through `register` with the test runner's `options`.

I checked it on screen with Claude Code 2.1.286 (`--plugin-dir`, the option set through `--settings` `pluginConfigs`) in a repository whose origin is `ssh://git@git.lab.lokkju.com/lokkju/demo.git`: a queued `[#12]` drew as an OSC 8 link to `https://git.lab.lokkju.com/lokkju/demo/issues/12`, the toast named the bad `oops` entry, and `/config` lists the row as "Forge hosts · session-decisions".

response.body:
Closes [#54](https://github.com/lokkju/skills/issues/54).

## Missing transcript cards

Terminal size wasn't the cause. On Claude Code 2.1.286 a TaskCreate call is folded into a `ToolGroup` with the calls around it (here the ToolSearch that loaded it), and a folded group of those draws nothing on the main view, so the `ToolUse` hook that draws the card never got a row to draw in; ctrl+o unfolds the run, which is why the card showed there. I saw the same thing at 80x24, 100x30, 120x40 and 160x50, fullscreen and main screen alike. A `ToolGroup` hook now draws the cards of the items its finished calls made under the group. An unfolded group is `ToolUse` rows, which already draw them.

`"tui"` in a `--settings` file does apply: `"tui": "default"` overrode a user-level `"fullscreen"`, and `CLAUDE_CODE_NO_FLICKER=1` overrode `"tui": "default"`.

## Clickable references

At session start the plugin reads the `origin` remote (or the only remote) with `git remote get-url`. On github.com, gitlab.com, codeberg.org, or a host named `gitlab.*`, `forgejo.*` or `gitea.*`, it turns `#N`, `!N` and `owner/repo#N` into URLs for that forge:

- the short link on the button row is a `Link` with the reference as its label
- references in the question and qualifier become markdown links
- the More dialog gets a `Link: <url>` line and **Copy link**

On any other host the references stay text, since a self-hosted forge's kind can't be told from its name.

I checked it on screen with term-record, using a scratch repo whose remote is `git@github.com:lokkju/skills.git`. The cast has OSC 8 spans for `!4` (`/pull/4`), `#9` (`/issues/9`) and `#12` (`/issues/12`). The dialog draws its question as plain text, and the cast shows the `Link:` line with no OSC 8 around it. That line is clickable only in a terminal that spots URLs in plain text on its own.
response.title: feat(session-decisions): link issue and PR references, and draw cards for folded TaskCreate rows

response.body:
More opens Claude Code's question dialog, which keeps every line break and wraps at the terminal width but draws no markdown. The plugin already stripped the markdown, but it passed the description through `excerpt()`, which cut it to 320 characters or six lines, and showed the recommendation only when the card's tag shortened it.

## What changed

- `dialogQuestion` (hooks/markdown.ts) builds the dialog text: the question, a blank line, `Recommended: <full recommendation>`, a blank line, then the description through `dialogText`, which keeps lines, blank lines and list items (`*`/`+` bullets become `- `, headings lose their `#`), drops emphasis and code markers, and writes a link as `text (url)` when the text isn't already the url.
- The 320-character/6-line cap is gone. The render hooks record `viewport.rows`/`columns`, and the description is cut to the rows left after the dialog's chrome: 12 rows (rule, header, blank lines, "Type something", rule, "Chat about this", hints, and the three-row task list under the dialog), plus one per option. Rows are counted as wrapped at the screen width less the dialog's two-column gutter. With no measurement, the question gets 24 rows. A cut ends with `… N more lines not shown`. Ruling D28: `/next` no longer fingerprints its facts on the newest Actions run `updated_at`. That value moved on every CI run in progress and threw away a saved slate for nothing.

The fingerprint now reads each open PR's head commit SHA and its combined check state (`pending`, `success`, `failure` and so on from the head commit's `statusCheckRollup`, or `none`). A new push or a changed check result still moves it. The new `OpenChangeHeads` query is a paginated read-only GraphQL query; it replaces the REST `actions/runs` read, so a small repo still takes four requests for the fingerprint.

- `forges/github.py`: `fingerprint_inputs()` drops `newest_pipeline` and adds `change_heads`.
- Tests: a pipeline `updated_at` change alone keeps the cached facts and the saved slate; a check state moving to success, failure or none, or a new head SHA, re-reads the facts and asks for a new slate. The cached run asserts no `actions/runs` request.
- The `/next` fixture is re-recorded read-only against lokkju/skills with `--record`.
- Spec and README list the new inputs; the spec's Decisions section records D28.

response.body:
Part of #24.

This adds `/next` for GitHub: the facts, the fingerprint cache, the classification, the unblock counts and the slate (phase 3 of `docs/specs/forge-tracker.md`). By the owner's ruling it comes before phase 2, so it depends on nothing phase 2 builds.

## What /next reports

`forge-tracker next` prints four parts. **Your queue** lists the person-only items, most agent-ready items unblocked first, each with why it's person-only and what it unblocks. **Agent lanes** groups the agent-ready items into lanes Claude judged shouldn't share files, each item marked in flight when it has an open PR (with its draft, conflict and CI state) or a pushed branch. **Blocked** lists each blocked item and what it waits on. **Flags** lists merged-but-open issues, links to closed blockers, blocked labels with nothing linked, blocking cycles, and pushed branches with no PR that name no issue. Until a slate is saved for the current facts, the agent-ready items are listed by tier, agent label, due date and number, and the report ends with `slate: needed`. `commands/next.md` then has Claude read `next facts --json` (which adds issue bodies), build the slate, save it with `next save-slate`, and rerun.

## How it classifies

Person-only means the needs-human or decision label (firm), or a `person_only_markers` word in the title or a label (a hint Claude may overrule in the slate with a reason). Blocked means an open blocker by native link, or the blocked label. Agent-ready means open, not person-only and not blocked (D19): the agent label only sorts items first within their tier. An assignee is never a reason for anything and shows as owner. Unblock counts walk open links with a visited set, so a cycle counts each item once; cycles are found with an iterative Tarjan pass and flagged. Merged-but-open uses real closing references only (`closedByPullRequestsReferences`), never `#N` in a title or branch.

The facts are cached in `next/<host>_<project>/facts.json` with a fingerprint of the cheap reads the spec lists, plus a hash of the config file. While it holds, a rerun makes four requests. A run with a failed read is written but never reused, and no slate is shown or saved over it. Every read fails on its own and none renders as empty: if the blocking links fail, items that would be agent-ready show as not classified; if the issues read fails, every section says FAILED.

## The phase-2 seam

Phase 2's pickup record (branch to issue) doesn't exist yet. `next.recorded_pickups` is the single place that would read it; it returns none for now, and `classify` already accepts pickups with `via: "pickup"` (a test covers that path). Until then, an issue is in flight only through what the forge shows: an open PR with a closing reference to it, `#N` in an open PR's title, or `N` as a segment of a PR's or pushed branch's name.

## Reads

The adapter gains two reads: `fingerprint_inputs` (one GraphQL query for the default-branch head, open counts and newest update times, plus paginated milestones and branch heads, plus `actions/runs?per_page=1`) and `closing_refs` (GraphQL over open issues; more closing references than one page holds is a FAILED read, not a short list). `Issue` now carries its body. All requests are GETs or GraphQL queries through the existing guard.

## Tests

`tests/test_next.py` builds a fake forge with a decision that unblocks a chain, a needs-human item, a marker hint, tiers and the agent label, an in-flight PR and branch, a merged-but-open issue, a blocked label with nothing linked, a stale link and a cycle. It checks the text report against a golden, the JSON classification, the 0600 cache and fingerprint reuse, `--refresh`, a config change moving the fingerprint, failed reads (never reused, never shown as empty, tokens redacted), the saved slate with its age, `--rerank`, a moved fingerprint, every `save-slate` refusal, and that `save-slate` touches no forge. There are unit tests for transitive and cycle-safe unblock counts, a 1500-item chain, marker word matching, cross-project blockers, pickups and branch-number parsing. A `/next` run recorded from this repo replays against a golden report, and the adapter's new reads join the contract suite. 196 tests pass on Python 3.9 and 3.14.

## Open questions

1. **A blocked label with nothing linked counts as blocked.** The spec's `/groom` treats it as drift and proposes removing the label; `/next` still treats it as blocked and flags it, since calling it agent-ready would trust the label less than the person who set it.
2. **The config file is part of the fingerprint.** The spec's list doesn't include it, but classification and the slate depend on its labels, tiers and markers, so a config change asks for a new slate.
3. **A blocked person-only item goes under Blocked, not Your queue.**
4. **Unblock counts walk through person-only items but don't count them.** If P blocks Q (person-only) and Q blocks A, P's count includes A.
5. **The newest pipeline time moves while CI runs.** That's in the spec's fingerprint, but it means a slate saved during a CI run goes stale when the run finishes. A per-commit check state (or excluding in-progress runs) would be steadier.
6. **Sub-issues aren't read.** The spec's table lists GraphQL `subIssues` next to `blockedBy`, but nothing says parent and child are a blocking relation, so only `blockedBy` counts.
response.title: feat(forge-tracker): /next on GitHub: your queue, agent lanes and what is blocked

The standing-backlog count line is missing whenever the count is zero.

`commands/catchup.md` says to keep the standing-backlog count line as it is. `render()` in `scripts/forge_tracker/catchup.py` prints `standing: ...` only when `waiting["standing"]` is non-empty, so a zero backlog prints nothing. A reader can't tell "nothing standing" apart from "the line was dropped". The first lokkju/skills catchup on 2026-10-15 had no standing line at all.

Fix: always print the line, as `standing: none (not updated in the window)` when it's empty. If the line is meant to be conditional, change the command text instead. Either way, add a render test.

response.body:
The `/catchup` header doesn't say the marker moved.

`commands/catchup.md` tells the reader that the report's first line says whether the marker moved. `render()` in `scripts/forge_tracker/catchup.py` only says so when the marker *stays* (`--no-mark`, or a read FAILED). In the normal case, where the marker moves, the header only names the basis: "(first catchup here: the last 7 days)" or "(since your last catchup)". Nothing says the next catchup starts at the window's end.

Seen on the first lokkju/skills catchup on 2026-10-15, which exited 0. Its header read `lokkju/skills on github.com, 2026-10-08 21:21 to 2026-10-15 21:21 (first catchup here: the last 7 days)`.

Fix: when `report["marker"] == "move"`, append something like `; marker moved to 2026-10-15 21:21`, and add a render test for each marker state.
